From Pop-up Pirate to Screwball Scramble, the Japanese toymaker Tomy became synonymous with mechanical puzzle games in the 1980s, and it's still going strong. It's just announced its first rebrand in 20 years, and it's the company's most radical identity change yet.

Tomy will have a new name for those of us outside of Asia. It's also introduced a new unified logo for all markets, and the dramatically different look has caused a lot of surprise.

See our guides to the best laptops for graphic design and the best monitors for graphics artists if you need new tools for your own work.

Tomy will now be known as Takara Tomy everywhere, consolidating its global branding under the name it was already using in Asia. In all markets, the familiar white and blue wordmarks are being replaced by a new logo design that combines the name with a rather abstract-looking symbol with a teal-to-magenta gradient. The company calls its colours 'Quality Blue' and 'Quality Gradation'.

While the symbol looks inscrutable, the company says it's based on a fusion of the katakana characters for 'asobi', a term that can be translated as 'play', 'recreation' or 'amusement' (see the video below). So although the logo looks indecipherable, it's actually a literal representation of the brand's playful spirit,

That playfulness is apparent in the wordmark too, if you look closely. There are two Ts, and three As in the company name, but each one is rendered different. The first A has a slight downward curve on the crossbar, the second a slightly upward curve, and the last has serifs on the feet and apex. From a distance, the wordmark looks fairly uniform and reserved, but each letter has its own personality.

However, some people aren't sure that the icon works. Even in Japan, people seem to be struggling to decipher its meaning.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

"Is it the chip on a credit card," one person wonders on X. "It looks like a seafood processing company," someone else thinks.

Some are even suggesting that the company's announcement that the new identity will be rolled out on 1 April 2027 is a sign that the rebrand might be an extremely early April Fool's Day prank.

I'd say it actually looks like a Screwball Scramble.

Here's the company's video explainer, which shows how the design was formed.

Tomy is an abbreviation of the name of Eiichirō Tomiyama, who founded the company in 1924. The company merged with Takara, another Japanese toymaker, in 2006. That led to the last rebrand, under which the company adopted the Takara Tomy name in Asia.

In an explanation of the rebrand on its website, Takara Tomy says it's now transforming from a 'toy company' to a 'play company' and that it will adopt the motto "One Takaratomy" as it unifies its branding".

#8992. Samsung P9 SSD Review: Finally Best in Class

Samsung P9 SSD Review: Finally Best in Class

I have been very hard on Samsung SSDs over the last few years. The T-series SSDs have been hugely popular among photographers because of their compact size, but I have never liked them because of their atrocious transfer speeds. For what they cost, they just aren’t worth it. But Samsung finally has me changing my tune.

Samsung has finally produced a slim, fast, and cost-effective portable SSD that is the best in its class.

Prior to the P9, Samsung used USB 3.2 Gen 2×2, which can provide peak speeds of up to 2,000 MB/s… as long as you’re using the right connection. Gen 2×2 has always been badly supported on all computers, but it is particularly badly supported on Apple devices, where a single Apple computer in the last decade supported it on just one of its USB ports.

Gen 2×2 was always meant as a stopgap between USB 3.2 and USB4, but manufacturers kept using it because it was cheaper than paying for the higher USB4 components, while it also let them claim super-high transfer speeds on the box. This was, for a majority of users, effectively a lie: most would never see anywhere near those speed promises and would instead cap out at sub-800 MB/s peak read and write speeds.

I was willing to forgive this back when the T7, T8, and T9 SSDs cost under $100, but these days the MSRP of these SSDs has ballooned to around or over $260 for 1TB and $1,000 for 4TB. That’s an insane price for such low performance, especially given the alternatives.

What I can never fault Samsung for is its SSD design: small, thin, and light. The T series got this bang-on, and the new P9 really does a good job with carrying that forward.

Samsung has slowly moved away from its rubber or silicone wrap that it put around the T7 as it evolved the series, and the latest T9 moved to a “carbon pattern” rubber that was significantly less thick. The P9 feels like the next logical step: fully moving away from that kind of a wrap and leaving the metal bare. This makes the design feel less rugged, but it is unlikely to make a major difference for most users in practice. Perhaps it won’t be quite as drop-resistant – and Samsung isn’t really talking about that at all, actually – but I personally prefer it. I just was not a fan of how the T series felt in hand.

There is really not a lot else to talk about with the design of this little SSD. It has a single USB4 port, an indicator light, a little embossed line for design effect only, and Samsung’s logo. Simple, light, straightforward, and svelte.

I will say that the corded USB cable that Samsung includes with the P9 is very nice and is a good length (about a foot long). It includes two Velcro cable ties to keep it organized in your tech bag, and it is wholly unbranded (which I also like).

If I had one knock on the P9 design, it’s that the all-metal exterior scuffs very easily. I put this P9 in my bag for one quick trip to Los Angeles earlier this month, and it has a pretty noticeable blemish now. People tend not to care about this too much, but if you’re someone who likes to keep their tech neat and clean, that might be hard with the P9.

As I said before, Samsung SSDs have always had a nice design, but the performance was woefully lacking. That finally changes with the P9.

As a recap, PetaPixel‘s storage testing involves speed testing SSDs brand-new out of the box, filling the SSD to capacity and testing again, and then emptying the SSD and testing a third time. We also have recently added Amorphous DiskMark to our Blackmagic Speed Test bench, but we continue to use the Blackmagic numbers in our historical chart for the sake of consistency.

The SSD I tested is Samsung’s 2TB capacity option.

These are great numbers, especially compared to Samsung’s previously woeful performance with USB 3.2 Gen 2×2. They are not close to the best we’ve seen out of other USB4 SSDs or Thunderbolt 5, but they’re very good. The P9 has support for first-gen USB4, so it caps out at 40 Gbps and won’t match the speeds of the Oyen U35 Bolt+ or the Glyph EX80, but it does compete well against the ProGrade PG10 and the Glyph EX40.

There is a dip in write performance when the SSD fills, which is worth noting, but its peaks are higher than both Glyph and ProGrade USB4 Gen 1 options. I think this matters even more when you consider the size and weight of the Samsung P9: it’s significantly smaller and lighter than other options in its tier. I could carry three P9s for around the same size and bulk as a single Glyph EX40, for example.

In use, the Samsung P9 is completely silent, which is expected given it has no moving parts, but it is also surprisingly good at sinking heat despite its thin and small chassis. It does get warm when under load, but that warmth doesn’t last for long and quickly returns to below body temperature and feels cold to the touch. I didn’t see any evidence of thermal throttling either. Overall, fantastic performance.

As often as I am hard on brands, I am willing to give praise when it is earned: Samsung has created an SSD that maintains all of the benefits of the T series while finally backing that up with performance. This is a fantastic little SSD that performs well. Somewhat surprisingly, it’s not crazy expensive either: $340 for 1TB. Compared to the $290 retail price of the Samsung T9 for the same capacity, it’s well worth it to jump over to USB4 for the $50 upcharge, as you’re getting way, way better speeds with the P9 versus the T9 (or T8 or T7).

This is still a worthwhile purchase even if you don’t have a USB4-compatible computer, since it’s better to invest in products that can grow with you rather than hold you back. The next time you get a computer, it’s more likely than not going to come equipped with USB4 support, and you will want to be able to take advantage of that instead of being left behind on USB 3.2.

As mentioned, the Samsung T series (most recently the T9) is going to be the most obvious direct competitor. It’s cheaper, but not by much and certainly not by enough to accept the huge dip in performance. The P9 is nearly five times faster than the T9 for an extra $50. To me, that’s a no-brainer.

The aforementioned Glyph EX40 is a direct USB4 (generation one) competitor, and it is significantly heavier and bigger and has worse performance in most circumstances. It is more consistent under heavy load, but many will see the much smaller P9 as a better choice to shed some weight. Additionally, the P9 is $100 cheaper than Glyph at the 1TB capacity. Both the EX40 and the P9 offer 2TB, 4TB, and 8TB options, and as the capacity goes up, Glyph’s price gets more competitive until it is actually cheaper at 8TB ($2,450 versus $2,700).

The ProGrade PG10 is in a class of its own since it is only available in the 16TB configuration right now, and if you need that much capacity, it is a more cost-effective option at $4,200 versus the $5,400 it would cost to buy two 8TB Samsung P9 SSDs. ProGrade’s PG10 is also slower, especially the 16TB version, which tested worse than ProGrade’s lower capacities it once offered.

Yes. Samsung has finally produced a slim, fast, and cost-effective portable SSD that is the best in its class.

#8990. Photographer Gabriel Moses to Receive the Trailblazer Award at The Fashion Awards 2026

Photographer Gabriel Moses to Receive the Trailblazer Award at The Fashion Awards 2026

Gabriel Moses — the photographer behind some of the most influential fashion campaigns in recent years — will receive the Trailblazer Award at The Fashion Awards 2026.

The British Fashion Council (BFC) announced that Gabriel Moses will receive the award at The Fashion Awards ceremony at the Royal Albert Hall in London on November 30.

Previous recipients of the Trailblazer Award include fashion designers Kim Jones, Sarah Burton, and Alessandro Michele — making Moses’ recognition a significant milestone as a photographer and highlighting his growing influence on the fashion industry.

“Gabriel is one of those rare creative talents whose work has an unmistakable visual language and emotional resonance,” Laura Weir, Chief Executive, British Fashion Council, says in a press release. “Across fashion, music, film and art, he has helped shape contemporary visual culture, while opening up new perspectives and inspiring a generation of creatives. We’re delighted to celebrate Gabriel at The Fashion Awards this year and recognise the extraordinary contribution he continues to make to British and global creative culture.”

A post shared by Gabriel Moses (@gabrielomoses)

Gabriel Moses is a British-Nigerian photographer and filmmaker from South London, known for his distinctive visual style and ability to turn deeply personal stories into striking images that have made an impact across fashion, music and art. Making his directorial debut with Nike at just eighteen years old, Moses established the foundations of a creative practice rooted in storytelling, identity and community. Entirely self-taught, he has since redefined the possibilities of contemporary image-making, making history as the youngest photographer to shoot a Dazed cover at just 22.

His creative portfolio spans campaigns and collaborations with some of the world’s most influential fashion houses and cultural institutions, including Louis Vuitton, Dior, Burberry and Moncler, alongside portraits of cultural figures such as Pharrell Williams, Jay Z, Rihanna, Lauryn Hill, Grace Jones, Cher, Travis Scott, among others. In 2024, Moses released his first monograph Regina.

“It’s a blessing to receive such a prestigious award, I’ve put a lot of heart into my practice from the moment I started and moments like this are a testament to honest work,” Moses says. “I’m grateful to the long list of collaborators who have trusted my ideas.”

This fan illustration features Kankuro, a character from Naruto. In such a large cast of unique ninjas, his special power stood out to me; he controls deadly wooden puppets with lines of energy! Finding the sketch that best communicates what’s important about a character is crucial to a successful illustration. You may want one of the best drawing tablets or the best laptops for drawing.

When I first started thumbnailing ideas for this piece, I focused on the basic composition and character posing, even if the perspective or proportions were a tad off. In this step, quickly putting ideas down is really important to get some flow; we can always tidy things up later.

After considering the geometric structure of the characters and redrawing everything, I nailed down the final line art using references for hands and other details. My goal is to avoid repainting or wandering in the rendering phase. This is the time to structure and define.

Using a textured brush, I’ll work on all the light-shadow transitions, making them softer. With this strong base, adding small highlights completes the 3D illusion. I balance the values to push some parts of the painting back, bringing the darkest parts forward, like the characters’ heads.

#8987. AI helps conservators uncover lost details in William Merritt Chase painting

A conservator works on William Merritt Chase’s A Comfortable Corner. AI helped reveal how the painting had changed over the years, including through earlier restorations Photo: Lindsey Del Rio for Modern Art Conservation

When William Merritt Chase’s painting A Comfortable Corner (around 1888) entered the conservation studio, the painting was carrying more than a century of history on its surface—including the interventions of conservators who had treated it decades earlier. Artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to a restoration endeavour that has peeled back some of those interventions.

The newly restored painting, which is part of the collection of the Parrish Art Museum in Water Mill, New York, will be on display in its exhibition William Merritt Chase and Walter Granville-Smith: American Impressionists of the East End (14 November-21 March 2027). The Parrish has an especially deep connection to Chase, who was not only a prominent figure in Gilded Age New York but also spent time on Long Island’s East End, where the museum is located. Today, the Parrish holds a substantial body of Chase’s work, alongside archival material donated by the artist’s family.

A Comfortable Corner depicts a woman reclining in an elaborately furnished interior, dressed in a deep blue kimono and holding an uchiwa fan.“A Comfortable Corner is an important work within William Merritt Chase’s oeuvre as it depicts a specific moment in 19th-century art and Chase’s own period with influences of art and design from Japan,” says Kaitlin Halloran, the museum’s associate curator.

Over the years, at least two restorations substantially altered the appearance of the painting, including a significant effort in the 1960s. Among the changes made were the addition of a heavyweight, almost burlap-like lining, retouching and blotchy inpainting, and the use of uneven varnishes. Some of these interventions changed the surface texture of various areas or discoloured over time. Working with conservator Suzanne Siano and her team at Modern Art Conservation, the museum set out to determine what restoration was needed to get the painting ready for the exhibition.

A crucial piece of evidence to guide this process arrived in the form of an early photograph of the painting. The black-and-white image, understood to have been taken before the 1960s restoration, showed that more of the composition had once been visible than what had survived in the painting. The work had apparently been reduced in size during the 1960s restoration, perhaps to fit a new stretcher or because damaged edges were folded over and effectively removed.

Conservators from Modern Art Conservation with William Merritt Chase's A Comfortable Corner (The Blue Kimono) (around 1888) Photo: Lindsey Del Rio for Modern Art Conservation

The photograph also revealed details in the composition that had disappeared. A curl of hair beneath the sitter’s ear was missing; parts of a decorative screen had become faint or vanished; and some delicate passages had been overpainted with heavier marks. The conservation team also found evidence of pentimenti—changes made by Chase himself—that were not apparent in the earlier photograph, adding another layer of complexity.

“It is difficult to establish whether all of these changes resulted from earlier conservation,” Siano tells The Art Newspaper. “Some of it may have stemmed from a misreading of what the conservator was seeing. They may have been cleaning toward what they believed to be the original surface when, in fact, some of what they removed may have been changes or additions made by the artist.”

Using AI, the historical photograph was combined with a colour image of the painting to create a composite showing areas where the two diverged.

“Although we are reasonably adept with Photoshop, we felt it was worth seeing what AI could offer,” Siano says. “It proved very helpful, largely because of its speed. It was not instantaneous, but it was considerably faster than assembling the comparison manually.”

The resulting image helped the team identify areas that warranted closer examination. One important discovery concerned Chase’s signature, which had become extremely faint, with some of its letters apparently covered by overpaint. Because Chase’s signature is relatively abstract, Siano believes it may have been mistaken for part of the carpet pattern during the earlier restoration.

The project, supported by a Bank of America grant, illustrates both the possibilities and the limitations of AI in conservation. “Tasks that once took considerable time can be completed more quickly, and AI can provide additional information for us to weigh,” Siano says. “Ultimately, however, conservation is carried out by a highly skilled individual or team, and we do not expect that to change.”

Siano stresses that they did not simply reinstate every discrepancy identified by the software. The historical photograph was neither high-resolution nor necessarily a record of the painting’s earliest state. Instead, the information the photograph provided was assessed alongside magnified examination, ultraviolet imaging, knowledge of Chase’s materials, and comparison with his other works.

“Conservation is a combination of science, art history, craft, manual skill and artistry,” Siano says. “AI is none of those things.”

The Chase painting was the first time Siano’s studio had used AI as an aid in the conservation of a painting. “In terms of determining how to conserve a painting, we think AI’s use will remain very case-specific. We do expect it to become increasingly valuable as a research tool, however: for example, in helping to locate historical images or relevant source material.”

Ultimately, Siano says, “the judgments conservators make are nuanced and subtle, and we doubt those qualities can be replicated by a machine”.

Alex Kachkine, a PhD student at MIT, art-lover and self-taught restorer, wanted to provide conservators with another “tool in the toolbox”

#8986. Photographer Can Take Jigsaw Puzzle Company to Court Over Use of His Photos

Photographer Can Take Jigsaw Puzzle Company to Court Over Use of His Photos

A photographer can proceed with his copyright infringement lawsuit against a Canadian puzzle-maker that allegedly used his images on its jigsaw puzzles.

Last week, a judge ruled that professional landscape and nature photographer Elliot McGucken could pursue copyright infringement and Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) claims against Canadian puzzle manufacturer Karmin International.

In his lawsuit, McGucken claims that Karmin International reproduced five of his photographs without authorization on its puzzles in its “Nature’s Beauty” series and placed their own copyright notices on the resulting products. The companies allegedly sold the puzzles across the United States, including in New York.

McGucken argues that this was misleading because the copyright notices suggested that Karmin International owned the rights to photographs that he had taken. He also alleges that the companies removed identifying and copyright information from his original images before reproducing them on the puzzles. McGucken alleges that the companies continued selling the products and displaying his photographs even after receiving notices from Shutterstock concerning the alleged infringement.

McGucken sued Karmin International, but the puzzle manufacturer asked the court to dismiss several of the photographer’s claims in his lawsuit. However, on November 3, Judge John G. Koeltl of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled that the photographer could proceed with most of his copyright infringement claims against the puzzle maker.

According to Vital Law, Judge Koeltl ruled that McGucken had provided sufficient grounds for his allegations that Karmin International used false copyright notices on the jigsaw packaging and removed identifying information from his original photographs.

The judge also allowed McGucken’s claim of vicarious copyright infringement to proceed. This means a company can potentially be held responsible for another party’s copyright infringement if it has the ability to supervise the activity and benefits financially from it. McGucken alleges that Karmin and its marketing affiliate Playview worked together to produce and market the puzzles and that they both benefited from the sales.

#8985. Speed, Drama, and Unapologetic Grain: The Case for Kodak T-Max P3200

Speed, Drama, and Unapologetic Grain: The Case for Kodak T-Max P3200

This Film Friday is featuring our favorite low-light film: Kodak T-Max P3200. T-Max P3200 is one of the fastest films you can load into your favorite 35mm camera and is perfect for a night out if the flash has to stay home or for just scratching that itch you have for superb contrast and graininess.

There are not many super-high-speed options out there in the film world. Ilford manufactures Delta 3200 (in both 35mm and 120, no less), and Kodak has T-Max P3200. Below that, you drop to ISO 800 in color and all the way to ISO 400 for the next fastest B&W film. Back in the day, we had Fujifilm Neopan 1600, Provia 1600, and Natura 1600, among a few other options, but those are long gone. So, the two 3200 films we have on the market fill an important role.

Kodak T-Max P3200 (TMZ for short) was originally introduced in 1988 as the third member of Kodak’s T-Max family of films, along with T-Max 100 (TMX) and T-Max 400 (TMY). The T-Max films are noteworthy for their T-grain structure. Similar to Ilford’s Delta films, T-grain films are designed to produce a smoother grain structure that has less grittiness to it and prints and scans more cleanly. But honestly, you will never think of T-Max P3200 as a fine-grained film—quite the opposite, in fact. But that’s OK, because its grain is one of the features we like best about it.

Let’s face it. T-Max P3200 is grainy, but grain is the price you will pay for speed. Our recommendation is to embrace grain, learn to appreciate it, and even love it. Grain is the building block of analog images; it is an integral part of how the photo is made. Once you come around to this, your love of black-and-white films will only grow and grow. And if you are already a fan of film grain, there are few films out there that will please you more than P3200. Buy this film for its grain and consider everything else it has to offer as icing on the cake.

Speaking of which, grain is not the only feature T-Max P3200 has going for it. Its other big strength is its speed. The film is marketed as an ISO 3200 film. If you do any sort of research into this film, you will quickly discover that it is really an ISO 800–1000 film (depending on how you develop it). The “P” in P3200 stands for “push”, as in that is what you are essentially doing with this film when shooting it at 3200.

Our suggestion? Forget all of that. It just causes confusion. Think of P3200 as an ISO 3200 film, because among the many things it does well is expose at ISO 3200. Rate this film at its box speed, go out into the dark, and odds will be good that you come home with decent exposures. This reliability at high speeds has long endeared T-Max P3200 to us. In contrast, while there are things we like about Ilford Delta 3200, we almost never expose it at ISO 3200, generally opting for a slower ISO 1600 or even ISO 1000 rating to help ensure decent exposures. In our experience, Delta 3200 needs to be paired with Ilford developers to really hold onto its speed, whereas P3200 doesn’t seem to be quite as picky. With T-Max P3200, we have no fear of rating it for those higher speeds.

And speaking of higher speeds, T-Max P3200 can actually go even higher. One of our own staff members set out on a mission to see how high he could take P3200. He got it up to ISO 102,400 before he felt like the process (either the film’s sensitivity or his developing) was breaking down. While his results at those absurdly high speeds are grainy beyond belief and have crunched shadows, they do an excellent job of showing the versatility of this film. Even if ISO 102,400 is not your cup of tea, rest assured that the film will handle ISO 6400 or 12800 pretty dang well.

So, you have grain and speed. The third element we love about P3200 is its contrast. T-Max P3200 has dramatic contrast. It is an atmospheric film. Pair it with dramatic light, and the results will be eye-catching. The shadows and highlights on P3200 tend to go toward the extreme, with the shadows getting crunchy and the highlights slipping into bleached white. In good hands, these qualities make for great images; just be mindful that, if the highlights or shadows are important to you, you should meter the image accordingly.

If you have stuck around this long, we’ll treat you to a little historical “bet you didn’t know”. If you have ever wondered why Kodak has never manufactured this emulsion in medium format, well… they did. They actually tried to make P3200 in 120 but ran into technical issues they could not fix.

Apparently, the emulsion of P3200 is so sensitive that the slight lip from where the tape connects the film to the backing paper was causing a slight pressure mark in the first frame. Kodak couldn’t eliminate it and figured they couldn’t market the film as an “11 exposure” roll film, so the idea got axed. But still, thinking about shooting P3200 in 120 keeps us awake some nights considering the possibilities.

So, that is our review of T-Max P3200. It is a film we use when we know we need the speed (low light). Or when we have an itch for grain and grit (texture). Or when we are hoping for a bit more contrast in our images (drama). We love T-Max P3200 and were heartbroken when Kodak discontinued it in 2012, and we were likewise elated when it was reintroduced in 2018. T-Max P3200 was given a reprieve from death, and all of us film photographers have benefited from its returning to the market. So make sure you have taken the chance to try a roll of it.

Hit up Blue Moon’s website via the link or visit our Portland, Oregon-based shop to enjoy a Film Friday discount on this wonderful film. Today only!

#8984. Exhibition explores how the fisherman-turned-artist Alfred Wallis inspired leading British artists

Boats at Quayside by Alfred Wallis and Christopher Wood (undated) Courtesy Hamilton Kerr Institute

Pallant House Gallery in Chichester, southern England, does not own any paintings by the self-taught Cornish artist Alfred Wallis (1855-1942). But it does own many works by the early 20th-century artists who were heavily influenced by the former fisherman and rag-and-bone merchant, who first took up painting with pots of house paint and sheets of cardboard as a lonely widower aged 70.

Alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist gathers together works by Wallis and by artists who visited, lived in or worked in St Ives, including Barbara Hepworth, Peter Lanyon, Margaret Mellis, Adrian Stokes, John Wells, Wilhelmina Barns-Graham, Ben and Winifred Nicholson and Christopher Wood. It was Ben Nicholson and Wood who first befriended Wallis in 1928 when they peered in astonishment into his tiny dark cottage stuffed with paintings.

Many of the Wallis paintings—of tilted houses and harbours, ships and stormy seas, under lowering grey skies—originally acquired as gifts or bought for a few shillings, are now being borrowed from private collections and museums including the Tate, Kettle’s Yard in Cambridge and Aberdeen Art Gallery. A private collector is loaning a unique collaborative work: a half-finished view of a Brittany quayside by Christopher Wood, which Wood gave to Wallis who then completed it.

A record price of £184,000 was set at a Christie’s auction last year for a work by Wallis, who once said to a buyer: “gimme what you like for ’em”. Ben Nicholson, barely earning himself and with a young family, bought his first Wallis painting for half a crown; Wallis once sent a bundle of paintings to the collector and curator Jim Ede for ten shillings. When the artist died in 1942, a roll of uncashed postal orders was found on his mantelpiece. He was only saved from a pauper’s grave by the St Ives artists.

Winifred Nicholson’s Seascape with Two Boats (1932) Photo: © Kettle’s Yard, University of Cambridge; © Trustees of Winifred Nicholson

The exhibition is curated by James Scott, an orthopaedic surgeon, who first discovered Wallis when, as a bored medical student, he spent days in Sotheby’s auction rooms, watching sales and afterwards tracing the buyers out of curiosity.

Scott insists there was neither condescension nor exploitation in the relationship between Wallis and Nicholson and the other art school educated artists. Hepworth wrote that Wallis never knew “how much we all learnt from him”.

The St Ives artists “discovered him when they were looking for a new direction, experimenting with a restricted palette and flattened picture plane,” Scott says, “and they found he was already doing it and doing it better.” Wallis learned nothing from them, continuing his own unmistakable style until weeks before his death.

Scott treasures two works by Wallis. “I’ve often thought maybe the time has come to sell them, and then I come downstairs and see them on the wall and think no, I can’t, I love them more and more.”

• Alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist, Pallant House Gallery, Chichester, 21 November-2 May 2027; Penlee House, Penzance, 15 May 2027-9 October 2027

The most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:

The "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

These definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

National income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

This explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

Income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

The FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

The financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

What distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

Income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

The distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

Whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

Add up all pre-tax income for your household — wages, self-employment, investment income, and any other sources. Compare to the Pew thresholds adjusted for your household size. For a three-person household, middle income is $56,600 to $169,800.

Use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

Your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most important predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

Multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

According to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

By national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, New York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

The Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

Pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

Income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

A brilliant, comfortable productivity mouse. The haptics and Actions Ring reward creatives who’ll map shortcuts, but Options+ takes work, and for most MX Master 3S owners or non-creatives, it’s a marginal upgrade.

Comfortable, well-judged weight with real desk presence

Special Edition colourway offers a touch of personality

Haptic feedback adds useful tactile confirmation

Actions Ring speeds up app switching and folder access

MagSpeed scrolling is still class-leading

Needs time in Options+ to get the best from it

Marginal upgrade over the MX Master 3S unless you map shortcuts to the Action Ring

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Product: Logitech MX Master 4 (Special Edition)

Sensor & Tracking: Darkfield high precision, 200-8000 DPI

Scroll: MagSpeed electromagnetic wheel plus thumb wheel

Connectivity: Bluetooth and Logi Bolt receiver

Software: Logitech Options+ (Windows and macOS)

Best for: creatives, office workers and anyone with long desk sessions

The MX Master 4 Special Edition takes Logitech's excellent black mouse and spruces it up with a new white colourway and red-and-grey accents. Inside, it's the same MX Master 4, and like the 2025 version, it has a tough act to follow. Its predecessor, the MX Master 3S, is already one of the best productivity mice you can buy, so Logitech never intended to reinvent the wheel. Instead, we get more customisation, haptic feedback, and a handful of design tweaks, and in this Special Edition, a more personalised colour choice.

These are all the developments I’d expect from a follow-up to the excellent MX Master 3S, one of the best mice you can buy, but they make this a nicer-looking version of a mouse that was a smart evolution rather than a must-have upgrade, unless, I'd argue, you're a creative; then the Actions Ring becomes a bigger thing than you may expect and is new to MX Master 4, Special Edition or not.

The shape is the same as the MX Master 3S, with its sculpted ergonomic design, deep thumb rest, and plenty of controls to keep your hands off the keyboard. It’s comfortable for long workdays, and the weight is spot on. It has enough heft to feel planted on the desk without feeling clumsy. It’s big, though, and it won’t suit everyone. This is a mouse for your desk, not your laptop bag.

• For more control consider one of the best drawing tablets

The MagSpeed wheel is as good as ever. Flick it, and it free-spins through a long spreadsheet or a 40-page document, then ratchets back to click-by-click scrolling when you need precision. Switching between the two is automatic, which is why it’s so easy to take for granted.

The finish is where things have changed. This is the Special Edition of last year’s MX Master 4 release, so the design changes over the MX Master 3S remain. Logitech has swapped the soft, rubberised coating of older models for something harder, but it’s not slick or glassy. The cover has a nice bit of tooth, and different areas have subtly different textures, so your fingers always know where they are without you looking. It feels different from the old MX Masters. A colleague wasn’t keen on it when they tried [2025’s MX Master 4], but I got used to it quickly, so your mileage may vary, and existing owners may need a few days to adjust.

Those alterations aside, the Special Edition replaces flat blacks with a soft grey-white colour and red accents. The dark grey Actions Ring thumb rest pops in this colourway, and I far prefer it to the faceless black PC-mouse aesthetic of the base model. There’s no price difference between black and Special Edition.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The thumb rest gets the biggest rethink. It’s usually the most wasted area of a mouse, a bit of plastic to rest your thumb on. Here, it’s the way into the new virtual dial, called the Actions Ring, which makes it feel like part of the design rather than an afterthought.

The haptics are a lovely touch. They kick in when you make a selection and when you open and cycle through the Actions Ring, so I can keep my eyes on the screen, click and scroll, and still feel a little resistance and feedback. This also helps with gesture control, too, if you go as far as needing that kind of input. It’s subtle, but it makes the mouse feel more connected to what you’re doing.

As you may have guessed, the Actions Ring is the real star of the new features. It’s an on-screen dial that expands what the mouse can do, making it easy to open folders or switch between apps without dropping into the Windows menus. You can tailor the ring to the job, from something as basic as Google to Photoshop or DaVinci Resolve. Support isn’t universal, though. The best digital art and design apps like Krita, Affinity Photo and CorelDRAW are covered, but smaller apps like Escape Motions Rebelle aren’t a default option, so you’ll need a workaround: assign function keys in Options+, then match them to the app’s own shortcuts for undo, clear layer or brush toggles. It works, but you need to know your keys or set them up ahead of time.

This also means getting to grips with Options+ and its app features, which is a lot of learning for a mouse. I’d like it to work more without that software running in the background. But if you persevere, it adds real depth and makes the mouse faster to use and more flexible. Once it’s set up, you’ll love it. You can tweak everything from haptic strength to scroll speed, and I’d probably be moaning if I couldn’t fiddle.

The haptics, gestures, and Actions Ring are a step beyond the MX Master 3S, and creatives who map shortcuts to the ring will get the most from this mouse.

So, should you buy the MX Master 4 Special Edition? If you’re coming from a basic mouse, absolutely. The ergonomics, scrolling and customisation make it a brilliant tool for anyone who works at a computer all day, whether in creative apps or simply navigating menus and Google.

If you already own an MX Master 3S, it comes down to how you work. The haptics and Actions Ring are genuinely useful and, for creative apps, a new, easier way to work, so it’s worth it if you’ll map shortcuts to the ring or, like me, hate sorting through Windows menus and would rather one-click into the regular apps and files. For everyone else, they’re not enough to make a perfectly good mouse obsolete.

#8981. I Spent Four Days With the Leica Q3 43 F1 Camera

I Spent Four Days With the Leica Q3 43 F1 Camera

Formula One has changed a lot since I’ve been watching. People used to look at me strangely when I said I enjoyed watching race cars drive around in circles on a Sunday. Now, the sport is swamped by new fans drawn to the sport via Netflix’s Drive to Survive and Charles Leclerc’s boyish good looks.

I hold no ill will towards this new generation of fans who I doubt can list every F1 World Champion going all the way back to the 1980s as I can. In fact, without them, I dare say I would never have received the limited edition Leica Q3 43 F1 edition in a brown cardboard box this week.

After news broke about the new camera, I simply had to try it. Photography and F1 have a history: Canon sponsored Williams in the team’s glory days; possibly my favourite F1 photo of all time is Nigel Mansell and Ayrton Senna glancing over at each other while driving almost 200 miles per hour in Barcelona in 1991. Their wheels are inches apart from each other, both daring each other to see who will brake first. The sponsor on Mansell’s wing reads ‘Canon.’

So far as I know, this is Leica’s first-ever foray into F1. The special version of the Q3 43 comes with carbon fiber grips, a material that’s both light and strong, which is why F1 teams have been using it to build cars for the past 40 years.

The camera comes covered in non-slip microvelour that’s modeled on a racing steering wheel. The pictures really don’t do this material justice; it’s a beautiful touch and I couldn’t stop running my fingers over it, like when you’ve just shaved your head.

That’s not all the F1-inspired hardware, either. The shutter is a soft-release button with a carbon inlay and red rim. It reminds me of an old-school stopwatch, the kind you’d see in a movie about a promising young rookie arriving for testing with an established team at a rain-soaked racetrack somewhere in England. He completes his first lap, the timekeeper clicks the stopwatch, glances at the time, turns to the engineers, and gives a knowing smile. You just know he’s going to be something special.

Having never shot a Leica Q3 of any focal length, I immediately fell in love with it. I mean, it’s just so damn beautiful. It’s a perfectly proportioned camera, and a joy to use. It took me no time at all to set up, and I particularly enjoyed the little ‘zoom’ button that crops into the sensor from the 60-megapixel 43mm to the five-megapixel 150mm end.

And it’s certainly a head-turner. I showed it to as many people as I could over the past four days, and everyone was taken with it. The BMXers were particularly impressed with the microvelour finish. My mom called it “handsome.”

I wanted to shoot some pulsating auto action with it, but I quickly realized that — despite the F1 logo on the front — it’s not exactly a camera for shooting high-speed objects. It’s still a Leica Q3; it’s a camera that wants you to slow down and think carefully about what you’re shooting. In his review of the Q3 43, Chris Niccolls said, “There is a simplicity and a meditative experience to be had, wandering the streets with a compact camera on your shoulder.” That is true.

As I write this, the camera is already on its way back to Leica. I will miss it. But at almost $10,000, it’s very unlikely I will be buying one.

#8980. How Understanding Animal Behavior Transforms Your Wildlife Photography

How Understanding Animal Behavior Transforms Your Wildlife Photography

Wildlife photography is about more than finding an animal and capturing a sharp image. Understanding animal behavior helps photographers anticipate movement, recognize meaningful interactions, and capture moments that reveal more about a subject than its appearance alone—they tell a story.

Most of all, taking the time before you even pick up your camera to learn how to read body language and recognize behavioral patterns can make the difference between reacting to an action and being ready when it happens.

A photograph can show an animal in beautiful detail, but behavior gives the image another layer of meaning and wow factor. The way an animal moves, feeds, communicates, interacts with others, or responds to its surroundings offers insight into its daily life. Capturing these moments helps tell a more complete story and gives viewers a better sense of the animal beyond its physical appearance.

Behavior also creates opportunities for more compelling compositions. An animal looking directly toward the camera can make an effective portrait, but a photograph of it displaying, feeding, preening, or interacting with another animal can communicate much more. These moments introduce action and context, giving the viewer something to interpret rather than simply observe.

Understanding behavior is particularly valuable because some of the most powerful wildlife photography sits at the intersection of storytelling and documentation of animals’ lives. Animals follow routines and respond to their surroundings according to instinct, environmental conditions, and social relationships. Photographers who recognize these patterns have a better chance of anticipating what might happen next and preparing to capture it.

One of the best ways to become a more effective wildlife photographer is to spend time learning about the animals you want to photograph before heading into the field. Wildlife documentaries, online videos, books, scientific articles, and species-specific resources can all provide useful information about feeding habits, courtship, territorial displays, migration, nesting, and other behaviors. Watching footage can be especially helpful because it allows photographers to see how an animal moves and how one action often leads to another.

However, learning does not have to happen entirely through research. Spending time observing animals in person is just as important, particularly when you can return to the same location regularly. Birds are a common and effective starting point because they are found in a wide range of environments and display an extensive variety of behaviors. Even a local park can offer opportunities to learn how different species feed, interact, defend territory, and respond to people or other animals. To keep things simple, I will focus primarily on birds throughout this article, as their visibility and varied habits make them ideal subjects for study.

When first learning about wildlife photography and animal behavior, simply sitting on a park bench with a book while casually observing nearby birds can be a useful exercise. Watch how they move through their environment, how often they pause to look around, and what they do before taking flight. Notice how their behavior changes when another bird approaches or when people move nearby. With repeated observation, familiar actions become easier to recognize, and you begin to notice patterns that might otherwise go overlooked.

Locations where large numbers of birds gather can be particularly valuable places to practice. For me, rookeries along the New Jersey shore provide opportunities to observe nesting activity, courtship, feeding, and interactions among birds. During winter, the gathering of bald eagles around Conowingo Dam in Maryland offers a chance to watch feeding behavior, competition, and interactions around fish. Areas of open water that attract wintering ducks and geese, including snow geese, are also useful observation sites. When many birds gather in one location, photographers can watch different behaviors happening simultaneously and compare how individual species respond to one another.

To find wildlife hotspots near you, research is key. Look up local Audubon chapters, birding groups, and guided trips—whether on social media or through organized photo walks at nature centers. These communities can be a great source of camaraderie, education, and field assistance.

The goal at these hotspots should be to observe just as much as to photograph. Rather than immediately concentrating on getting a particular image, spend time watching the birds and learning what is happening around you. Notice where they tend to gather, when activity increases, and how they respond to changes in their surroundings. Most of all, returning to the same location can reveal patterns that are difficult to recognize during a single visit.

Animals communicate through more than vocalizations. Posture, movement, positioning, and subtle changes in appearance can all provide clues about what an animal is doing or how it is responding to something nearby. Learning to recognize these signals helps photographers distinguish ordinary activity from moments that may lead to an interesting interaction or display.

Birds provide many visible examples. Changes in posture, feather position, head movements, and wing displays can indicate courtship, aggression, alertness, or preparation for flight. A bird that repeatedly looks in one direction may be responding to another animal or monitoring a potential threat. A change in stance or a sudden pause can also signal that its attention has shifted.

Recognizing these signals also gives photographers time to prepare their camera settings. If a bird begins shifting its weight, lowering its body, or opening its wings before taking flight, it may be time to increase the shutter speed and switch to a continuous autofocus mode if you are not already using one. If two birds begin displaying toward each other, consider widening the composition and checking that your shutter speed is fast enough to freeze sudden movement. Small adjustments made before the action begins can make a significant difference.

Hunting herons and egrets are great subjects to practice on, as they methodically scour shallow water to snatch up prey. This predictable, repetitive behavior gives you time to observe, learn, and test your own “hunting” skills.

Once photographers become familiar with an animal’s routines, they can begin anticipating what it may do next. Many wildlife behaviors follow recognizable sequences, even though the exact timing can vary. An animal may pause before moving, shift its posture before taking flight, or display a series of movements before interacting with another individual. Recognizing these patterns creates opportunities to prepare for the photograph rather than simply reacting after the action begins.

Camera settings should reflect the behavior you expect to photograph. For a stationary bird or mammal, a shutter speed around 1/500 second is often a useful starting point, although the appropriate speed depends on the focal length, subject movement, and camera stability. For walking animals or birds that are moving more quickly, 1/1000 second can provide a better chance of freezing motion. Takeoff, flight, running, and fast interactions may require 1/2000 second or faster, particularly when you want to preserve detail in wings or other rapidly moving parts.

For example, when photographing eagles gathering around a feeding area, a bird preening on a branch may be relatively easy to capture at 1/1000 second. However, if you are anticipating a takeoff or an interaction over a fish, increasing the shutter speed to 1/2000 or 1/3200 second can help freeze the action. Birds in flight against a relatively clear background may also be easier to track with continuous autofocus and subject recognition enabled, depending on the camera system.

Aperture is another important consideration. When photographing a single animal, a wide aperture such as f/4 or f/5.6 can help separate the subject from a distracting background while allowing more light to reach the sensor. However, when photographing two animals interacting, a slightly narrower aperture may provide enough depth of field to keep both subjects sharp, particularly if they are not positioned on the same focal plane. The trade-off is that a smaller aperture may require a higher ISO or slower shutter speed.

Auto ISO can be useful when photographing unpredictable behavior. Setting a minimum shutter speed and allowing the camera to adjust ISO as light changes can help maintain the speed needed to freeze movement. In rapidly changing conditions, this can be more practical than trying to adjust exposure manually while following an animal. It is still worth keeping an eye on the ISO, especially in low light, to avoid introducing more noise than necessary.

Another useful option is to configure a custom camera button or shooting mode for unexpected action. I set up what I call an “oh heck” setting, which switches my camera to its widest available aperture, a shutter speed of 1/2000 second, continuous autofocus, and burst shooting. When an animal suddenly takes off, starts fighting, or begins an interaction, I can press one button and have the camera ready for action without having to change several settings while the moment is unfolding. Many cameras offer customizable buttons or saved shooting modes that can be configured in a similar way. The exact settings can be adjusted to suit your camera, the subjects you photograph, and the conditions you typically work in, but having a ready-to-go action setup can make a real difference when something happens without warning.

Autofocus settings should also reflect the situation. Continuous autofocus, often called AF-C or AI Servo depending on the camera manufacturer, is generally the better choice when an animal is moving or likely to move. Animal subject detection can help maintain focus as the subject changes position, while a suitable tracking area gives the camera enough flexibility to follow its movement. For a stationary animal, a smaller focus area may offer more precise control, especially when branches, reeds, or other foreground elements could interfere with subject detection.

Composition needs to account for movement as well. If you expect an animal to take off, leave room in front of it rather than placing it tightly against the edge of the frame. When photographing feeding or social interactions, a slightly wider composition can preserve the surrounding context and keep important parts of the action from being cropped out. You can always refine the composition later, provided the original file retains enough resolution.

Anticipation also requires flexibility. Wildlife does not always follow predictable patterns, and an animal may change direction or abandon an activity without warning. Avoid becoming so committed to one expected moment that you miss something else happening nearby. Keep observing the entire scene, even when you are focused on a particular subject.

Some of the most engaging wildlife photographs involve more than one animal. Social interactions can reveal communication, cooperation, competition, courtship, and relationships between parents and young. These moments often provide a stronger sense of the animals’ lives than an isolated portrait because the photograph captures a relationship or exchange.

Photographing interactions requires paying attention to more than one subject. Watch how animals position themselves in relation to each other, how they respond to movement, and whether an encounter is developing into a larger display. The most meaningful part of an interaction may happen quickly, so it helps to anticipate the sequence rather than concentrate exclusively on a single frame.

Camera settings can become more challenging when multiple animals are involved. If two birds are interacting at close range, a shutter speed of 1/1600 to 1/2500 second can help freeze sudden movements, while an aperture around f/5.6 or f/8 may provide more depth of field than shooting wide open. The exact combination depends on the available light and how far apart the subjects are. If one animal is closer to the camera than the other, even f/8 may not provide enough depth of field to keep both sharp, so consider your shooting angle and focus placement as well.

Autofocus can also be less predictable when animals overlap or move across one another. A camera may switch focus between subjects, particularly when they are close together. If subject detection struggles, adjusting the autofocus area or using a more controlled tracking zone can help. Keeping a little extra room around the interaction also gives you flexibility if the animals move unexpectedly.

It is worth watching what happens after an apparent interaction ends. Animals may continue communicating, move together, or return to a familiar routine. Staying attentive beyond the most obvious action can lead to photographs that reveal more about the relationship between the subjects.

Knowing what is typical for a species helps photographers recognize when something worth capturing is about to happen. Familiarity with everyday routines makes changes in activity easier to notice, whether that means an interaction, a shift to feeding behavior, or a response to changing environmental conditions. Learning about the species and observing it over time provides a more reliable basis for understanding what is happening.

One example that I often use in my work is that ducks preening in the water often dunk their heads, shake, and then flap their wings to dry off. Knowing this sequence allows me to capture a signature “angel wing” pose time and time again across various species.

Developing an understanding of wildlife behavior takes time. A single outing may provide a few useful observations, but returning to the same locations allows photographers to build a more complete picture of an animal’s routines. Seasonal changes can also influence behavior, making familiar locations worth revisiting throughout the year.

Repeated observation helps photographers become more selective. Instead of photographing every movement, they begin to recognize which moments are likely to produce meaningful images. They may also become more familiar with the best times and locations for observing particular activities, making future outings more productive.

For example, while photographing screech owls, I have often found them resting in tree cavities during the day, but the real action and behavior of these nocturnal predators are best photographed at dusk.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra)

Patience is an important part of this process. Not every visit will result in a memorable photograph, and some of the most useful outings may involve spending more time watching than shooting. That time is still valuable. It builds familiarity with the animals and makes it easier to recognize opportunities when they arise.

Above all, respect for wildlife should remain central to every outing. Maintain appropriate distances, follow local guidelines, and avoid disturbing animals around nesting, feeding, or resting areas. The objective is to document natural behavior, not change it.

Understanding wildlife behavior changes the way photographers approach their subjects. Instead of concentrating only on finding an animal and achieving a technically successful exposure, they begin paying attention to routines, body language, and the relationships between individuals and their surroundings.

The knowledge gained through research and repeated observation makes it easier to anticipate meaningful moments and prepare for them. Whether watching birds at a neighborhood park or spending time at a seasonal gathering, photographers can develop these skills without traveling far from home.

The strongest wildlife photographs go beyond showing what an animal looks like — they capture a glimpse of how it lives. By learning to read behavioral cues, anticipating action, and approaching every subject with patience and respect, photographers can turn fleeting encounters into compelling stories.

Before it was an animated smash, Dispatch was a live-action browser experiment with a hard technical limit and one very durable doughnut scene. AdHoc’s founders explain the pivot.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A year ago, Dispatch released a game that surprised many people, including me. It's a superhero game about managing reformed villains from behind a desk, launched on PC and PlayStation 5. It has since garnered over five million players, and a mobile version arrives on iOS and Android on 9 December, following October's Dispatch anniversary Deluxe Edition.

Dispatch was made in Unreal Engine and stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as former hero Robert Robertson, alongside Jeffrey Wright, Laura Bailey, and members of the Critical Role cast. It's an animated, episodic workplace comedy that plays like a TV series, but it wasn't always a game, and that's perhaps why it feels so unique. AdHoc was founded in Los Angeles in 2018 by Telltale Games alumni who planned to make interactive experiences with real actors on screen, and Dispatch began that way.

I asked co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO and both co-creative directors, what survived the jump from live-action series to animated game, and what had to change.

One piece of the original script made it through every draft: the doughnut shop scene in episode two. Lenart says it was "one of the pieces from the early script that just kind of kept hanging around through every draft all the way from live action into the animated game".

The set-up was different back then. You watched a camera feed as the hero Invisigal dealt with a thief, and your job was to feed her the information she needed to succeed. In the live-action version, that meant switching cameras and pulling information from what each camera showed. Herman says the scene was "purely built around the technology" AdHoc was using to create its interactive live action. It ran in a browser and had hard limits, including, as Herman recalls, “I think it was like four simultaneous tracks of video”.

The team turned that restriction into a mechanic. Watch the alley behind the shop, and you couldn't see what was happening inside the front. "By choosing where you were going to give your attention, the game would adjust, and you'd learn different things based on where you were looking," says Herman, calling it the perfect place to test the idea.

Because they'd spent so long on it, they carried it forward. In the game, Lenart says, they wove in mechanics from the final design, such as hacking, "to make it feel a little bit more like Robert was helping out Invisigal".

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The original story was a mentorship, centred on the one-on-one relationship between Robert and Invisigal. Pivoting it into a game changed that. AdHoc wanted a dispatch mechanic, with the player sending heroes out on calls, and that needs a roster. "So the Z-Team was created to support the gameplay," Lenart says, "which then informed the story, and then changed the overall arc of the season, which brought a whole team into it as opposed to just a one-on-one mentorship with Invisigal."

It's a neat illustration of how the studio works. "Everything at AdHoc starts with story," says Herman, contrasting that with studios that pick a genre first, polish the mechanics and the game-feel, and only later ask what the story is. AdHoc begins with the world, the characters and who the player is, then asks what that means for gameplay. "Oh, well, you're a superhero dispatcher, so maybe we should have some sort of dispatching mechanic, right?"

Once there's a script, it moves on to storyboards, animatics and animation. That storyboard stage is now part of the product: the anniversary Deluxe Edition update adds Storyboard Mode, which plays the whole game through its original animatics. It's a new mode that offers genuine insight into how a scene was planned, scripted and animated.

The move to animation was driven by budget constraints, to an extent, because they could do more with a little extra, and it also changed the game's scale, given Dispatch's live-action origins; Lenart says the team knew they were "severely limited from a budget standpoint compared to big-budget superhero tentpole movies". For budgetary reasons, the story was largely set in an office with a small cast.

Animation flipped that constraint and aligned with trends like Mixtape's hand-made animation, giving the team room to grow and aim higher within the new art form. "We're able to have a giant action scene because it doesn't cost that much more than having a bunch of characters walking around talking," Lenart explains. That let AdHoc expand the moments that deserved spectacle: "Let's really go all out and try to compete with some of the other best-in-class versions of these scenes in animation."

Ask whether players have done anything that made AdHoc rethink how interactive stories should work, and Herman is refreshingly honest. “I don’t know that there have been any major epiphanies,” he says, before steering to a different answer: launching Dispatch “was a labour of love”, the culmination of a lot of work distilled into one experience the team felt was exciting and high quality.

He adds: "The success of the game has just really injected a lot of confidence into us and other developers making similar types of games. For a long time, there hadn't been a really clear or recent example of something like this reaching a level of success that a developer could go out and raise funding for."

He's proud of who found it, too. Dispatch "was able to pierce a new audience who perhaps thought gaming wasn't for them". Lenart agrees, saying the success feels like "motivation to keep making these types of games and expand our possibilities even more".

The Dispatch Deluxe Edition is out now on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and Nintendo Switch / Switch 2, and $10.99 digital upgrade path for existing owners

#8977. Images of Marilyn Monroe by Her Last Surviving Photographer to Be Exhibited

Images of Marilyn Monroe by Her Last Surviving Photographer to Be Exhibited

An upcoming exhibition will feature photographs of Marilyn Monroe taken by Lawrence Schiller, the last living professional photographer to have worked with the Hollywood icon.

Schiller is the last surviving professional photographer to have worked with Monroe. He even saw the actress on the morning of August 4, 1962, the day she died at age 36, to discuss an upcoming photo shoot.

To mark the centennial of Monroe’s birth in 1926, The New York Historical will present Marilyn Monroe Centennial: Photographs by Lawrence Schiller, which will be on display from November 20, 2026, through March 28, 2027.

Although Monroe’s image has been reproduced countless times during her lifetime and in the decades since her death, the exhibition offers a closer look at how she managed her career and public image. Featuring 36 of Schiller’s photographs alongside his personal recollections, the exhibition explores Monroe’s efforts to shape how she was seen by the public.

The New York Historical’s photo exhibition juxtaposes the star’s on-camera and off-camera persona with images taken by photojournalist Schiller on two film sets, Let’s Make Love in 1960 and Monroe’s last and unfinished film Something’s Got to Give in 1962.

While on assignment in Los Angeles for Look and Paris Match magazines, Schiller, then a young photographer, found Monroe to be a knowledgeable collaborator rather than simply a subject. Keenly aware of the power of imagery, Monroe showed Schiller how best to capture her.

“You’re already famous, now you’re going to make me famous,” Schiller said to Marilyn in 1962 as he and Monroe discussed the photos he was about to take of her on the set of Something’s Got to Give.

“Don’t be so cocky,” Monroe replied, “photographers can be easily replaced.”

Among the photographs on display is a series Schiller took during production of Something’s Got to Give. During a scene filmed on a closed set, Monroe spontaneously decided to remove the light nude-colored bikini bottoms she had been given and resurface naked. The resulting images, showing Monroe in the film’s swimming pool, appeared on magazine covers in more than 30 countries, including the cover of Life magazine.

Other photographs in the exhibition explore several defining aspects of Monroe’s 16-year, 30-film career in Hollywood. These include her efforts to be recognized as a serious actor, her relationships with acting coaches Lee and Paula Strasberg, and her attempts to gain greater control over her career. During her career, Monroe’s efforts to challenge the traditional studio system and become one of the first women in Hollywood to establish her own production company.

“Marilyn Monroe remains the definition of an icon, a sparkling presence on screen and a powerful storyteller in her own right who fought against the forces of her time,” Dr. Louise Mirrer, president and CEO of The New York Historical, says in a statement. “While it’s true that Marilyn Monroe experienced great adversity and exploitation in her time, she also displayed remarkable resilience, sharp instincts, and physical mastery to ensure the camera captured her to her best advantage.

Dr Mirrer adds: “This exhibition attempts to showcase that agency through Lawrence Schiller’s exceptional photography, enlightening personal stories, and archival analysis drawn from our extensive collections.”

More information about The New York Historical’s upcoming exhibition Marilyn Monroe Centennial: Photographs by Lawrence Schiller can be found here.
