#8976. Is the Nikon D850 Really as Good as You Remember, or Is It Just Nostalgia?

Is the Nikon D850 Really as Good as You Remember, or Is It Just Nostalgia?

I never owned a Nikon D850, although I put some miles on my D700 over the years. I did get a chance to review the D850, though, on one of my first major press trips to Bend, Oregon. This was back in the TCS TV days, and it was there that I met many of the industry professionals who I now consider good friends.

That's a good place to start, because my time with the D850 is steeped deeply in good memories and nostalgia. It got us wondering... Was this the case for everyone else too, or is this camera actually as good as we remember?

It’s quite rare to have reviewed a digital product almost ten years ago and find that it is still available today brand new. When KEH said they had a D850 to lend us, I happily agreed to revisit this legendary camera and focus more on the shooting experience than on a proper review.

The D850 wholeheartedly deserves its legendary status. It was the pinnacle of Nikon DSLR technology, combining a relatively compact chassis with a high-res 45.7-megapixel sensor. I loved composing images through the brilliantly clear viewfinder with 100% coverage and the 2.3-million-dot LCD panel with full tilt articulation.

This is an SLR that could focus quickly, track faces and subjects with 3D-tracking technology, and fire bursts up to 9 frames per second with the right grip and battery combination.

The chassis is fully weather-sealed and made out of solid magnesium, with all the controls required to customize the camera and handle difficult shooting scenarios. Professional shooters will also appreciate the dual card slots for a CFexpress Type B card and a UHS-II SD card.

This is also a bit of a hefty camera, weighing almost 35 ounces (1 kilogram) when you throw a card and battery in. Most full-frame mirrorless cameras will weigh well under this amount, although Nikon seems to like heavy cameras, with the Z8 being the most similar, in both function and weight.

Regardless, the Nikon D850 is a pleasure to shoot, and it feels like the sophisticated tool that it is. It also happens to take some incredibly high-quality images, thanks to a sensor that may have been way ahead of its time.

It's amazing to think that a sensor placed into the D850 can still outperform modern mirrorless sensors in terms of raw dynamic range. Now, to be fair, the improvement is minor, and modern sensors read out way faster than they ever did. However, the fact is that the D850 sensor easily stands shoulder to shoulder with any full-frame camera today.

When we say that sensor technology has plateaued in the last decade, this is the perfect example. The D850 has a base ISO of 64, gathering extra amounts of light when possible, and will deliver incredible dynamic range and low-light performance. If you are looking for a rugged camera that can push shadows and pull highlights to the extreme, the D850 is a perfect choice.

Considering that the D850 can be purchased brand new for much less than a Nikon Z8, and that there is also a very healthy used market where the pricing gets even better, the D850 could make real sense to a photographer who doesn't necessarily need the mirrorless advantage.

That mirrorless advantage will largely manifest in terms of video performance, autofocusing sophistication, and more compact bodies and lenses. However, this isn't to say that the D850 is particularly weak in these regards either. I don't get the ability to autofocus anywhere within the frame, but the D850's coverage is still quite plentiful.

The 3D tracking works great even for inanimate objects, and there are plenty of situations where a single focus-and-recompose technique is all you need. Video is also fairly underdeveloped in the D850, with 4K resolution being available but somewhat soft-looking. The autofocus when using Live View is also abysmal, which was the standard for almost any non-Canon DSLR at the time.

However, there is a large market of photographers who don't care about video, don't need advanced subject-tracking autofocus, and don't mind a larger camera system. You won't get IBIS, but there are plenty of optically stabilized lenses available, and I found the shutter and weight of the camera to be solid and easy to hold steady even at slower shutter speeds.

Perhaps one of the strongest reasons to consider the D850 is just the joy of using an SLR camera as a different shooting experience. I had this same enjoyable realization when shooting the Canon Digital Rebel, and that camera is nowhere close to the D850's league. Composing with a premium viewfinder and having a powerful focusing system make the DSLR experience even better, and you don't have to break the bank to do it.

For the same price as an entry-level Nikon Z5II body, the Nikon D850 would give you a lot of performance for your money, along with an arguably more enjoyable shooting experience. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Deals on the console to play the year's biggest Nintendo game.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Nintendo Switch 2 is finally seeing some proper discounts, just in time to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, although you'll need to look beyond the US for the best deal. Woot, the Amazon-owned discount retailer, has dropped the price of Nintendo's latest console to $469, saving $30 off its $499.99 US retail price. The catch? You'll need an Amazon Prime subscription to get the discount.

It's not a massive saving, especially since Nintendo's 'next gen' console used to be cheaper than Switch 2's new US price, but discounts on Nintendo hardware are still relatively rare. For comparison, the console and Ocarina of Time bundle is $568, so it's cheaper to buy the Woot deal and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time separately, since it's $49.99 as a digital download. (That's $10 less than the physical edition.)

There's also a growing selection of UK deals to consider, and as with the US, it's rare to see Switch 2 drop in price outside of big sales events like Black Friday – it feels like Nintendo really wants you to play Ocarina of Time.

Amazon UK lists the standard Switch 2 through third-party sellers, with prices starting at £399.99 on its current listing, although the cheapest visible offer is a Like New console for £369.99 rather than a new console from Amazon itself.

Elsewhere, Sports Direct (yes, they sell Switch 2 and Nikes) has been listing the standalone console for £395.99, while EE has it for £405. Even better, EE has a Switch 2 and Mario Kart World bundle for £409, making the extra £4 a no-brainer if you don't already own the game.

Very is also worth a look, with its standalone console listed at £389.99, alongside bundles including Ocarina of Time, Donkey Kong Bananza and Mario Kart World. My pick? The Switch 2 Console bundle with Nintendo Switch Sports Resort and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, as you get the console's biggest game and the latest party game. The same bundle is £489 at Currys.

Speaking of which, one of my picks at Currys is a Switch 2 and Splatoon Raiders Bundle, spotted for £424 – it's one of my favourite Nintendo games released this year (read our Splatoon Raiders review to discover why). That's a particularly tempting option if you're after a game as well as the hardware.

The Woot deal is excellent if you're already an Amazon Prime member or want to join before Black Friday. But it does suggest there could be deals around the end of November for the year's big sales event.

If you just want The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, buying it digitally 'saves' you $10 off the physical edition price.

In the UK, I'd be looking at the £390–£410 mark for a Switch 2 console, especially bundles that include a full-price game for very little extra. There are more offers around right now, too.

#8974. Bangladeshi Photographer wins $200,000 for “Family” in the World’s Richest $1 Million Photo Contest

Bangladeshi Photographer wins $200,000 for “Family” in the World’s Richest $1 Million Photo Contest

Recognized as the world’s most lucrative photography competition, the 15th annual HIPA awards celebrated its winners on November 10, 2026, with Family as this year’s theme. The awards were presented at the Museum of the Future, the torus-shaped architectural landmark in Dubai’s financial district in the United Arab Emirates. The 15th season has been a landmark for the Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum International Photography Award (HIPA). Over 1,000,000 photographs have been submitted, over 500,000 photographers have participated, and 209 countries have been represented cumulatively since the competition started in 2011.

This season featured five categories: Family, Portfolio (Story-Telling), Sports Photography, General (B&W and Color), and Dreams Through AI, which was a newly created category in response to public demand. Judge Tara Todras-Whitehill, an award-winning photojournalist from the US, quickly pointed out that it is better to keep AI-generated work in a separate category rather than have participants enter it in regular categories.

The other notable judges were Ivan Pedretti, an Italian professional photographer; Kurt Mutchler, a former Senior Science Photo Editor at National Geographic; Germany’s Laci Perenyi, who has captured 21 Olympic Games; Sami Alramyan, a Kuwaiti documentary and humanitarian photographer for 20 years; American Santiago Lyon, Head of Advocacy and Education for the Adobe-led Content Authenticity Initiative; and Tomasz Tomaszewski, an acclaimed Polish photojournalist, with a Ph.D. from the Academy of Fine Arts in Warsaw.

His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum presented the $200,000 Grand Prize to photographer Pinu Rahman. His early-morning drone shot captured a family sleeping in their fire-devastated home, showing resilience and the human spirit.

Ali Bin Thalith, HIPA’s Secretary General, acknowledged the pivotal role of His Highness Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum in advancing the organization’s mission, recognizing his enduring commitment to promoting HIPA and fostering the global art of photography.

Here are the winning photos and videos of the 2026 competition, along with titles and descriptions submitted by the participating photographers.

Banker and amateur photographer Pinu Rehman bagged the Grand Prize for Under the Same Sky submitted to the Family category.

On 25 November 2025, a large fire broke out at around 5:20 p.m. in Korail, one of Dhaka’s most densely populated informal settlements. Spreading rapidly through narrow lanes of tin, bamboo and wooden structures, the blaze destroyed approximately 1,500 homes and left thousands displaced. Photographed the following morning from above, a family of five sleeps side by side within the surviving concrete walls of their burned home. Around them lie twisted corrugated tin, charred debris, and the remains of neighboring shelters. A few salvaged belongings are gathered close. With their home gone, the family rests together in the only space still available to them.

The First Prize in Family went to Hamid Obaid Al Ali for The Promise of Tomorrow.

Captured during a macro dive, this rarely witnessed underwater moment shows a tiny female sponge crab sheltering, her claws curled protectively around a dense cluster of developing eggs. The amber mass of eggs, each containing a life not yet emerged, rests against the textured surface of the sponge as the crab holds her position in the surrounding darkness. She will remain with her brood until the young are ready to enter the open ocean, where only a few will survive to adulthood. It is a reminder that parental devotion exists throughout the natural world, in places rarely seen.

The Second Prize was received by Nawaf Alosaimi for The Line.

A large herd of African elephants moves together across an open, darkened plain beneath a pale, cloud-streaked sky. A great matriarch leads from the front, her long tusks prominent and her wrinkled skin rendered in fine detail by the monochrome light. Younger elephants and calves press close among the adults, their trunks and legs forming a dense, overlapping mass of movement. Low hills and distant mountains sit along the horizon and a solitary elephant trails at the far edge of the frame, suggesting the full scale of the group crossing this vast, sweeping landscape.

The Third Prize went to Subhajit Datta for Framed Connection.

A glass window on a cruise vessel in Ha Long Bay, Vietnam, becomes both mirror and membrane. A father’s reflection fills the frame, camera raised, while inside a mother and child sit together at a dining table, absorbed in a quiet moment. Beyond the glass, limestone karsts rise from the water and other vessels drift in the distance. Reflection, transparency and light combine interior and exterior into a single seamless image, holding three members of a family together within one composed and layered frame.

The First Prize was bagged by Filip Hrebenda for What the Earth Draws in Secret.

Seen from altitude, the landscape abandons all pretense of the familiar. Glacial channels thread across dark sediment in luminous arcs, their turquoise indifferent to the gravity that shaped them. Along a ridge between shadow and a burning yellow ground, bare trees stand in silhouette — neither quite rooted nor quite free, caught at the threshold between dormancy and something that resembles beginning. The photograph does not celebrate renewal so much as observe it in its raw, unfinished state: a world mid-sentence, still composing itself, legible only to those willing to look from far enough away.

Franco Banfi claimed the Second Prize for Give Me a Ride.

A split-level view reveals an Olive Ridley sea turtle (Lepidochelys olivacea) resting at the surface of the open ocean while a Brown booby (Sula leucogaster) stands perched upon its olive-green shell. This well-documented yet unlikely relationship sees seabirds using surfacing turtles as floating platforms to roost and to feed on fish that gather beneath them. The turtle, protected as a vulnerable species, is the most abundant sea turtle in the Eastern Tropical Pacific. The arrangement offers a degree of mutual benefit: the booby gains a resting spot, while its presence may alert the turtle to approaching hazards.

Ramiro Torrents won Third Prize for Between Ice and Galaxies.

At Laguna Torre, near El Chaltén in Patagonia, a rare convergence of conditions produced this panoramic night scene. The sky cleared completely, placing the arc of the Milky Way directly above the mountains, while soft moonlight shaped the landscape below. In a region notorious for violent weather, the wind dropped entirely, leaving the icebergs motionless on a still surface. The composition preserves the true scale and immense depth of the wilderness, holding a fleeting moment of absolute stillness in a landscape defined by change.

Taking home the First Prize honor was Jono Allen for Mahina and Mother.

Mahina, meaning “moon” in Tongan, is an albino humpback whale calf, a rarity estimated at one in 40,000. Her luminous white body rests close against her mother’s dark, barnacle-marked skin, the contrast between them striking and immediate. The two are at the start of a 4,000-mile migration to Antarctic waters, accompanied by a chosen male guardian. Active shipping lanes, ghost nets, killer whales, and great white sharks mark the route ahead. Mahina’s white coloring, visible from great distances, heightens the dangers. Her mother and guardian remain close, their protective instincts attuned to her exceptional vulnerability.

The Second-Place award went to Barun Sarkar for Beyond the Threads.

Three children peer through a curtain of tangled threads, their faces only partially visible behind the dense weave. Each face is held at a different depth—two side by side and one smaller figure below—their eyes directed outward with quiet intensity. The threads, loose and cascading, partially obscure yet cannot fully conceal the children’s gazes. The strands represent more than fabric: they stand for poverty, limited opportunity, and the barriers inherited across generations. Yet each pair of eyes remains fixed on what lies beyond, carrying hopes that the threads cannot contain.

The Third Prize was awarded to Thomas Vijayan for Black is Powerful.

Out of the quiet depth of night, a melanistic leopard moves forward along a lit track, wild grass bordering the path beside it. The animal emerges from near-total darkness, its pale eyes fixed and unwavering. Reflected light traces the outline of its form, revealing powerful musculature and the faint marks of old scars. The monochrome atmosphere deepens the contrast between the illuminated ground and the surrounding blackness, giving the scene a stillness that speaks to the leopard’s natural authority as one of nature’s most elusive predators.

The winner of the First Prize was Chi Hui Tang for Between Heaven and Earth.

A snow-covered mountain stands beneath a sweeping lenticular cloud formation, its grand form perfectly mirrored in a glass-still surface where mountain, cloud and sky dissolve into one another. A lone black horse gallops across the vast expanse; its small, dark form the only movement within an otherwise tranquil scene. The landscape exists as a dreamlike vision of absolute stillness, freedom and the enduring, elemental forces of nature.

The Second Prize category winner was Fan Ho Tsang for Dreams We Inherit.

A high-speed train cuts through a tunnel of light, its sleek white form held sharp against streaks of blue and silver that radiate outward in every direction. The composition exaggerates the qualities of motion, light and perspective to carry the feeling of collective purpose—of generations moving forward together, each one building on the hopes and sacrifices of the last. The train becomes more than transport; it stands as a shared journey through time, carrying the weight of family and the inherited dreams they pass on.

The Third Prize was claimed by Bernardo Hernandez for Surfing the Sunset.

Along the beaches of Coveñas, Sucre, Colombia, a female surfer balances naturally atop a small breaking wave at sunset, warm light reflecting off the sea’s surface. The composition places the human figure in harmonious dialogue with the motion of the ocean, where the liquid textures of the water and the precision of the ride meet seamlessly within the warm, fading glow of the South American shoreline.

Yousef Alzanoon clinched the First Prize for Between Hunger and Fire.

“The weight of war in Gaza unfolds in its most unsparing dimensions. Flares illuminate the city skyline at night, while buildings collapse in clouds of smoke and people move through rubble-strewn streets. Thousands gather around aid trucks, carrying sacks of flour across a landscape marked by destruction. Women press forward with empty cooking pots. Aid packages descend by parachute over coastal tent settlements, while families flee on horse-drawn carts carrying their remaining possessions. Mothers hold severely malnourished infants, and children bear the visible effects of acute starvation. The unfolding crisis bears witness to the profound scale of civilian suffering endured throughout the conflict.

The Second Prize was won by Brent Stirton for Rewilding Rhinos.

“African Parks Network has assumed operational control of the world’s largest captive rhino breeding project, formerly owned by breeder John Hume, which houses over 2,000 southern white rhinos and more than 200 black rhinos. Following the operation’s bankruptcy, ownership was transferred to African Parks as a matter of urgency. The organization now faces the enormous challenge of translocating these animals to secure sites across Africa to bolster threatened populations, all while combating a relentless poaching epidemic. The narrative documents the scale and complexity of what may be the largest rewilding of an endangered species in history.

Don Pettit claimed the Third Prize for Milky Way from Orbit.

“These star-field time exposures were captured from the International Space Station using a customized, homemade sidereal star tracker. Rotating once every 90 minutes, the device counteracts the orbital motion of the ISS, allowing distant stars to be recorded as sharp, fixed points, something previously impossible in orbital photography. Across the expanse, Earth’s thin atmosphere glows with auroras in violet, crimson and gold, while city lights streak across the darkened surface below. The dense core of the Milky Way rises beyond the curve of the planet, with the structure of the ISS appearing in silhouette, a reminder of the human presence from which these views were made possible.

The First Place was won by Hongbin Wu for Winter Game.

“After heavy snowfall covered the mountainous Guoluo region of Qinghai, China, a group of young lamas cleared the basketball court at their temple and began an impromptu game. The concrete court forms a small island amid the surrounding snow, its dark surface contrasting with the vast white landscape. Dressed in scarlet robes, the young monks gather across the court, some playing while others watch from the edges. Their long shadows stretch across the ground beneath the winter sun. The quiet surroundings and lively game create a striking glimpse of youthful energy within the remote setting of monastic life.

The Second Place went to Faisal Hamada for Blazing Lap.

“A McLaren Formula One car speeds across the circuit beneath a blazing sunset, its trajectory stretching the surrounding light into horizontal bands of amber, gold and deep black. The car appears small and sharply defined against the environment, while its papaya livery blends with the warm tones of the sky. Motion blur transforms the circuit and surrounding atmosphere into sweeping lines of color, emphasizing the speed of the passing car. Against the intensity of the sunset, the highly engineered machine becomes a fleeting silhouette, capturing a dramatic moment where precision, movement and light converge.

Third Place went to Kirill Kudryavtsev for Celestial Flare.

“During the men’s snowboard slopestyle qualification at the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games in Livigno, Valtellina (Italy), Germany’s Noah Vicktor launches into the alpine air above Livigno Snow Park. A luminous circular glow surrounds his airborne figure against a deep cobalt sky. The groomed slope cuts a sharp diagonal across the mountainscape, while Vicktor appears suspended at the center of the natural sun flare. The flare creates a striking contrast between the precision of the competition and the expansive mountain landscape, transforming a fleeting sporting moment into an almost celestial scene.

Véronique de Viguerie is a French photojournalist whose work explores the grey zones of a world too often portrayed in black and white. For more than twenty years, she has worked in conflict zones and societies marked by war, repression and political upheaval, from Afghanistan to Yemen, Iraq, Somalia, Nigeria, Syria and Mali. Yet war itself is not her subject. What interests her is what survives within it: desire, humor, beauty, absurdity, tenderness, resistance and the rhythms of ordinary life.

She does not photograph beauty in spite of war. She photographs beauty, desire, humor and color because they, too, are part of war. To exclude them would be to create another kind of distortion.

This conviction has shaped her longstanding relationship with Afghanistan, which she first visited in 2003 and later lived in for four years. She has returned repeatedly to document Taliban fighters, civilians, women, families, and the profound transformation of Afghan society.

Her work on women has become increasingly central to this vision. De Viguerie is particularly interested in women living within restrictive or violent systems who are too often represented solely through what is done to them. Her photographs instead explore what they do: how they negotiate, resist, love, organize, protect and reinvent themselves, sometimes claiming power in spaces from which they have long been excluded.

Dr. Ali Mohamad is a photographer, documentary filmmaker, educator, and entrepreneur whose work is driven by a passion for visual storytelling and the creative industries. He founded TechMission, a digital media and production platform based in Dubai and serving the GC, alongside an education platform dedicated to empowering aspiring and professional photographers and videographers. Drawing on his industry experience, he shares practical knowledge that bridges technical expertise with creative vision, helping photographers and filmmakers refine their skills, develop their visual language, and approach their craft with greater confidence and purpose.

Kazuyoshi Nomachi (b. 1946) is an internationally acclaimed documentary photographer whose work explores the relationship between humanity, nature, and spirituality. Since his first journey to the Sahara in 1972, at age 25, he has devoted his career to documenting the lives, beliefs, and traditions of people inhabiting some of the world’s most challenging environments.

His journey to the Sahara profoundly changed his direction. Moved by the strength of people living in its harsh environment, he turned to photojournalism and began a lifelong exploration of humanity’s relationship with the natural world.

Inspired by the contrast between the Sahara’s aridity and the life-giving power of water, Nomachi began documenting the Nile in 1980. He traced the White Nile and followed the Blue Nile, capturing the extraordinary landscapes and communities shaped by these great rivers.

From 1988, Nomachi turned his attention to Asia. His work in western China introduced him to Tibet’s high-altitude communities and the spiritual traditions of Tibetan Buddhism. Between 2004 and 2008, he explored the sacred origins of the Ganges, documenting the landscapes and traditions central to Hinduism.

From 1995 to 2000, Nomachi photographed the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia, documenting the Hajj pilgrimage and the profound devotion of Muslims gathering in Mecca. Beginning in 2002, he explored the Andean highlands of Peru and Bolivia, examining the blending of Catholicism and Inca cultural traditions, a project he has continued to pursue.

Among his many honors are the Photographic Society of Japan’s Annual Award, received in 1990 and 1997, and Japan’s Medal of Honor with Purple Ribbon, awarded in 2009.

#8972. Tate’s Bloomsbury group exhibition throws fresh light on early British enthusiasm for Van Gogh

Self-portraits by the Bloomsbury painters: Vanessa Bell (around 1915) and Duncan Grant (detail) (around 1920)

Adventures with Van Gogh is a weekly blog by Martin Bailey, The Art Newspaper's long-standing correspondent and expert on the Dutch painter. Published on Fridays, stories range from newsy items about this most intriguing artist, to scholarly pieces based on meticulous investigations and discoveries.

Explore all of Martin’s adventures with Van Gogh here.

Tate Britain’s exhibition Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, which opened yesterday (12 November), emphasises how early 20th-century British artists were inspired by Van Gogh.

Vanessa Bell (1879-1961) and Duncan Grant (1885-1978) lived together for more than 50 years in a very Bloomsbury fashion, each having other lovers. The Bloomsbury group, named after the London quarter where they lived in the early 20th century, began as an informal collective of progressive artists, writers and intellectuals.

As the Tate show’s curator, Thomas Kennedy, points out: “When Bell and Grant were doing new and exciting things, individuals like Van Gogh—who were creating something wildly different from other artists of the time—were very much an inspiration for them.”

Bell and Grant were both also very close to the art critic Roger Fry, who in 1910 curated the pathbreaking London exhibition Manet and the Post-Impressionists, inventing the term Post-Impressionism. This show introduced Van Gogh to a British audience.

As so often with the Bloomsbury group, sexual relationships were complex and intertwined. In 1907 Vanessa had married the art critic Clive Bell, but it was always an open marriage. Two years later she started a relationship with Duncan Grant, producing a daughter, and they then continued to live together.

Duncan Grant, however, was homosexual, having numerous lovers, including a male cousin and Vanessa’s brother. To add to the complications, Vanessa later had a brief relationship with Roger Fry. The quip about the group was that they were “living in squares [in Bloomsbury], painting in circles and loving in triangles”.

The Bloomsbury relationships may seem bewildering to outsiders, but the key point to bear in mind with the current Tate exhibition is that Bell and Grant shared a home for over 50 years. Initially they lived in London, and, from 1916, partly at Charleston farmhouse in rural Sussex.

It proved to be an enduring artistic partnership. They influenced each other, and they, in turn, were influenced by modern European artists, such as Van Gogh, along with Paul Gauguin, Paul Cezanne, Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso.

The impact of Post-Impressionism: Duncan Grant's The Mantelpiece (1914) and Vanessa Bell's Still Life on Corner of a Mantelpiece (1914)

Grant, who studied art in Paris in 1906, may have then come across the work of Van Gogh. What is more certain is that Bell discovered Van Gogh in 1909, in a group exhibition at London’s New Gallery, which included a single painting by the Dutchman. She once described it as “a lovely little Van Gogh of flowers in a jug”.

The still life had been lent by Thomas Fisher Unwin, a London publisher who, with his wife Jane, had in 1896 been the first Briton to buy a Van Gogh after the artist’s death. This was a flower still life, probably one with a black background which has always been in private collections.

Van Gogh’s Bouquet of Flowers (summer 1886)

private collection (formerly Galerie Schmit, Paris)

But what was most influential for Bell and Grant was Fry's first Post-Impressionist exhibition in 1910. Including around 30 works by Van Gogh, it was the first chance for Londoners to see more than an odd painting by the artist.

This was a heady time for the Bloomsbury group. Bell later recalled: ”That autumn of 1910 is to me a time when everything seemed springing to a new life - a time when all was a sizzle of excitement, new relationships, new ideas, different and intense emotions all seemed crowding into one’s life.”

Catalogue of the second Post-Impressionist catalogue (1912), co-designed by Bell, Grant and Fry

Bibliothèque de l'Institut National d'Histoire de l'Art, Jacques Doucet collections

In 1912 both Bell and Grant had paintings in Fry’s second Post-Impressionist exhibition. They also co-designed the catalogue with Fry, and Bell helped hang the show. This time there was only a single Van Gogh, but it was again the Fisher Unwin flower still life, which Bell had known from four years earlier.

Bell, Grant and Fry all loved the south of France, where Van Gogh had also worked, and they visited regularly from the 1920s. Fry helped a friend buy a farmhouse in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, just a few hundred metres from the asylum where Van Gogh had stayed in 1889-90. On one occasion Grant visited Bell, who had bought a house just outside Cassis, on the Mediterranean coast. Grant described the surrounding landscape as “far more extraordinary than St Remi [sic]”. Both artists were well aware of Van Gogh's connection with Provence.

How then did Van Gogh’s art inspire Bell and Grant? They never set out to simply imitate his style, but were nevertheless powerfully influenced by his work and that of the other Post-Impressionists. The two British artists began to paint with heightened colours, simplified forms and strong lines.

The links can also be seen in individual pictures. Bell’s View into a Garden (1926, Bolton Library & Museum Services) includes two empty chairs, which were probably a reflection of Van Gogh’s pair of paintings of his own chair and the armchair of Gauguin (the picture of his own chair had been bought by London’s National Gallery three years earlier, so would have been well known to Bell).

In 1911, the critic Frank Rutter described Bell’s Chrysanthemums (1920, Tate, although not in the current exhibition) as “undoubtedly influenced by Van Gogh”. Its dark background echoes the Van Gogh still life which Bell had seen some years earlier.

Decades later, in 1946, Grant wrote to Bell about visiting a Van Gogh exhibition in Copenhagen, “a splendid show”. He added: “I really feel that artists should resist to the death having their works reproduced in colour. It really has been the death of Van Gogh. It’s only when one sees the originals that one realises what a very lovely & personal colour sense he had… I really do not believe in his madness as an artist at all.” Van Gogh remained in the minds of the couple for the rest of their lives.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

Buy Now Pay Later services let you split a purchase into installments — typically four payments over six weeks (Afterpay, Klarna "Pay in 4") or monthly payments over 3-36 months (Affirm, Klarna financing). The checkout process is seamless: enter your name and email, get instantly approved, and walk away with your purchase having paid only the first installment.

BNPL providers make money in two ways. First, they charge merchants 4-8% of each transaction — significantly more than the 2-3% credit card processing fee. Merchants accept this because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50%. Second, some providers charge interest on longer-term plans, and nearly all charge late fees when you miss a payment.

The "interest-free" label on short-term plans deserves scrutiny. While you may not pay interest, the behavioral cost is substantial. Research from multiple financial studies shows that BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction than they would with cash or debit. The psychological separation of the purchase from the full payment removes the natural spending brake that keeps budgets in check.

The financial industry has known for decades that separating the moment of purchase from the moment of payment increases spending. Credit cards exploit this. BNPL takes it further by making the payment feel even smaller — "just four easy payments of $37.50" feels dramatically different from "$150" even though it is the same amount.

A 2026 survey found that 43% of BNPL users have missed at least one payment. Among those who missed payments, the average person missed three or more over the prior year. Late fees compound quickly — four missed $8 Afterpay fees on a $200 purchase adds $32, effectively creating a 16% surcharge on what was supposed to be interest-free.

The credit score impact is evolving rapidly. As recently as 2022, most BNPL activity was invisible to credit bureaus. That has changed. Affirm now reports all payment activity to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna reports financing plans to all three bureaus. On-time BNPL payments may slightly help your score, but missed payments can drop it significantly — and the damage lasts up to seven years.

For anyone pursuing financial independence, BNPL represents the opposite of the FI mindset. FI is built on intentional spending, high savings rates, and letting compound growth work in your favor. BNPL encourages impulsive spending, fragments your cash flow, and creates obligations that reduce your ability to invest.

There is exactly one scenario where BNPL is financially rational: a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you would have paid the full price regardless. For example, you need a new dishwasher, you have the $800 in savings, and the retailer offers four interest-free payments. You keep your $800 invested for six more weeks while paying in installments. The benefit is tiny — a few dollars of investment returns — but the cost is genuinely zero if you make every payment on time.

Outside this narrow scenario, BNPL is almost always a worse choice than the alternatives.

The financial independence community is nearly unanimous: BNPL is a trap disguised as convenience. The entire BNPL business model depends on you spending more than you planned. If you were going to buy the item anyway and you have the cash, just buy it. If you do not have the cash, that is your budget telling you something important.

The question to ask before any BNPL checkout: "Would I buy this right now if I had to pay the full price in cash today?" If the answer is no, BNPL is not helping you afford something — it is helping you overspend. If the answer is yes, just pay cash and skip the installment tracking, the payment reminders, and the risk of a missed payment damaging your credit.

For those building toward financial independence, every dollar matters. The 30-50% spending increase that BNPL encourages directly reduces your savings rate — the single most important variable in determining how quickly you reach FI.

The average ChooseFI listener saves $24,000+ with an expert student loan plan.

Trusted by Brad Barrett, Co-founder and Host, ChooseFI

Mortgage lenders are increasingly scrutinizing BNPL obligations during the underwriting process. Multiple active BNPL plans — even if interest-free — show up as recurring liabilities and can affect your debt-to-income ratio. If you are planning to apply for a mortgage or auto loan in the next 6-12 months, pay off all BNPL balances and avoid opening new ones. Lenders view fragmented installment obligations as a sign of cash flow stress, even if you have never missed a payment.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Affirm is a legitimate, publicly traded company (AFRM on NASDAQ). It is safe in the sense that it will not steal your money or identity. However, being legitimate does not mean it is a good financial decision. Affirm's interest rates range from 0-36% APR depending on creditworthiness, and the company reports all payment activity to credit bureaus.

Increasingly, yes. Affirm reports to Experian and TransUnion. Afterpay reports to Equifax. Klarna financing plans report to all three bureaus. On-time payments may help slightly, but a single missed payment can significantly damage your score and remains on your report for up to seven years.

Afterpay charges an $8 late fee per missed payment, capped at 25% of the order value. After multiple missed payments, your account is suspended, the balance is sent to collections, and the delinquency is reported to Equifax. Collections accounts damage your credit score severely and remain for seven years.

Klarna's "Pay in 4" plan is interest-free with no late fees, but your account may be suspended for missed payments. Klarna's longer-term financing plans charge 7.99-33.99% APR, involve a hard credit pull, and report to all three credit bureaus. Read the terms carefully — the word "Klarna" covers very different products.

It is possible but unlikely for most people. Research consistently shows that BNPL increases spending by 30-50% per transaction. If you have the discipline to use BNPL only on planned, budgeted purchases at 0% interest — and never miss a payment — the financial harm is minimal. But for most users, the behavioral cost exceeds any convenience benefit.

Because it works — for the store. Merchants pay BNPL providers 4-8% of each transaction (vs 2-3% for credit cards) because BNPL increases average order values by 30-50% and reduces cart abandonment by 20-30%. The merchant is paying for you to spend more. That should tell you who this arrangement benefits.

Buy Now Pay Later is a marketing innovation designed to make you spend more — and the data confirms it works. BNPL users spend 30-50% more per transaction, 43% miss payments, and the credit reporting implications are growing. The only responsible use case is a planned, budgeted purchase at 0% interest where you already have the cash. For everyone else, especially those pursuing financial independence, BNPL is a detour in the wrong direction. Pay with cash, invest the difference, and let compound growth work for you instead of against you.

Linsoul’s IEM sale is truly impressive, and I've heard (and loved) 10 of the 13.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As the 11/11 sale swings into early Black Friday discounts, I've found 13 (mainly) in-ear monitor (IEM) deals that I'd personally buy today – in fact I already own 10 of them, so I don't think you can get a stronger recommendation!

All of the below wired earphones are distributed by the IEM retailer, curator, and distributor Linsoul, and with that comes a certain guarantee of quality. Everyone I've tested from them has hit a high level of quality control, so really all you as the potential buyer have to worry about, is if the sound profile is to your taste.

As I've tried most of them, I'm going to give you my tuning impressions, plus any design and comfort highlights for each of them. Many of them feature in my list of the best IEMs under $500, and my favourite budget IEMs under $100 – so these aren't just random IEM deals, but rather a curated list of genuinely excellent options.

I were to pick only one? Considering price, sound and build quality, I would get the Kiwi Ears KE4 down from $199 to $169. It's a fantastic, modern IEM that has a best-seller since its 2024 release for very good reason.

The Kiwi Ears KE4 is the one I'd recommend to most people out of all of these IEMs. That's because it has such a deliciously detailed midrange, and loads of bass (though admittedly too much for me sometimes). For $200, it's great value, and real audiophile quality. Read my full Kiwi Ears KE4 review.

The Horizon is for those that want more detail, and can handle more treble than most IEMs. Some will find it too bright, but it's just on the right side for me. With a detailed bass and decent midrange, things may be touch lean, but they are also separated and detailed. Read my Ziigaat Horizon review.

I really like these, and especially because they're only $50 – well, $42 now! For a fun, V-shape sound signature, that's a really great price, and though things get a little fatiguing after a while with the Cadenza II's full upper mids, it's still a very good IEM for under $50. Read my Kiwi Ears Cadenza II review in full.

Now you're talking... $315 may seem like too much for many people to be spending on a pair of earphones. All I can say is, if you want the best balanced tuned IEM on the market, then this is it, and that's the price for entry. Honestly, Crin could have put the price up considerable, and I believe it's great value at the discounted price.

Like bass?! Yeah, so does HBB, and although he's made several IEMs with different brands, the Deuce is one of the most beloved. I certainly think the wads of bass bring detail as well as head-throbbing amounts. But the rest of the frequencies are well-tuned too. Definitely not for everyone, this, but it's the best basshead set I've heard yet.

This is one of my favourite IEMs to date. It's bassy and warm without losing impact in the lower end, or detail in the lower mids. There's plenty (too much?) upper treble, but I find it all very nicely balanced. It's lush, warm and musical, and I love it. Read my Xenns Tea Pro review.

This IEM is fun, fun, fun. There's plenty of bass and treble, and it is a straight down the road V-shape tuning, but there's just enough detail and richness in the midrange to bring this out of the low-brow, commercial-style fare... I think its discounted price of $250 is good for this IEM.

I haven't heard this IEM, but like I say, Linsoul promises a level of quality that makes me confident in telling you about this deal. For $65 its promised reduced treble sound like an interesting approach – it's often the opposite for cheaper IEMs. Worth a punt!

I'm really interested in the Avant, as it's the first IEM that's made from Linsoul with the Linsoul brand in the name. Remember, Linsoul makes THeiaudio, Ziigaat and Kiwi Ears – that is, a lot of the best IEMs on the market today. Can't wait to hear these.

Want a pair of warm/neutral over-ear, open-back headphones? Well the Cypher is a good option, especially if you value great quality build. I found the sound to be a little soft in my Cypher review, but I can still see it being someone's ideal all-rounder.

The Halcyon IEM is a good option for those wanting that elevated treble that brings more detail to music, and who values a very small shell size. These things are tiny! I found them comfortable enough, but at the retail price I thought the Binary EP 321 were a better option. At the new sale price of $220, I think they're worth considering. Read my Kiwi Ears Halcyon review.

#8969. Nuart Aberdeen 2026: Poetry In The Streets

Welcome to the latest edition of Nuart Aberdeen. As far as we can ascertain, this will be the first street art festival in the world with a focus primarily on poetry and text-based works. Over the years, for better or worse, the large scale colourful figurative mural has come to dominate the culture we work with, and although it’s an aspect of the culture we support, due to the resources required to produce murals, they’re perhaps also the least democratic form of art on the streets. As curators, researchers and producers working in “festival” culture, we have a responsibility to not only showcase and celebrate the most interesting and technically competent works of our time, but to also ensure the culture’s development and survival. The only way to do this, is to inspire and encourage those without the privilege of a fine art degree or access to the arts, to have a go themselves. This has always been Nuart’s primary goal, not just to produce art, but to also inspire and produce the next generation of artists. A lofty goal, particularly as it’s often in conflict with the stated needs of sponsors and partners, on paper at least, and no one stands in front of a Tower block mural and thinks, I’ll pop home and have a go myself on the gable end of Gran’s house.

What we do have evidence for, is that the smaller, more human scale works – the stencils and paste ups and interventions – do have this effect. You could say that the ease of copying a Banksy stencil, which requires no more than a craft knife, a piece of cardboard and an idea, is the very foundation of this culture. We’ve seen this happen time and time again. Indeed, several of the producers and artists joining us this year, started their artistic journey as assistants and volunteers at Nuart.

At Nuart, we’ve always prided ourselves on not only showcasing the BIG names in muralism, but on also using the festival as a place to explore and experiment with new forms and ideas that engage with the idea of the whole city as a canvas, and not just the wall. In this respect, Nuart Aberdeen have been fortunate enough to have the support of some of the most thoughtful and progressive partners that an event such as Nuart could possibly have, and this year is no different.

Whilst pondering this issue, how to balance the needs of partners, tourist boards, with the need to impress the public, and create works of curiosity and interest for scholars which inspire the next generation, I imagined a city without art on the streets, with no forms of public expression, where all art is concealed behind the walls of city institutions and under guard 24/7. And then I recalled a piece of graffiti sprayed on the walls of Paris during the 1968 student uprising, an event which saw waves of creative energy explode onto the streets. It read, “La poésie est dans la rue”, or “Poetry is in the Streets” – could we harness some of this energy at Nuart to revitalise and energise the culture?

A short while later, I remembered a quote from pioneering UK graffiti writer Mode2. He was discussing how graffiti culture had taken hold and blossomed in the UK in the 1980s, and in a throwaway quip had said, the reason it took hold was because regardless of how interested you were in making art at school, if you couldn’t draw or paint realistically, you were bottom of the class. Then graffiti came along, and it struck everyone that all you had to know to create and engage with it, was your ABC’s.

And that was it. It was these two quite innocuous events that formed the genesis of this year’s poetry and text based Nuart. These are forms of creative expression that we all have access to and I hope the festival sparks the public’s imagination in the same way that those early bubble letters and Banksy stencils did.

Thank you as ever to all of our sponsors, partners and to the city council, for allowing us once again to make a contribution to what we believe is a magical and inspiring city.

— Martyn Reed, Nuart Founder and CuratorArtists include: Alisa Oleva (UK) Ciarán Glöbel (SCT) dr.d AKA Subvertiser (UK) HICKS (UK) James Klinge (SCT) KMG (SCT) Molly Hankinson (UK) Remi Rough (UK) Robert Montgomery (SCT) The Rebel Bear (SCT) The Writing Is On The Wall (UK) Trackie McLeod (SCT)  V2k | (LT - SCT)

#8968. After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins

Democratic leaders need to understand that cultural funding cannot stop at large museums and institutions; it must reach the people whose labor makes it possible.

In the afterglow of the blue-nami, those of us who make, organize, fund, and sustain cultural life are feeling a twinge of hope. But I find myself slipping into a spiral of anxiety as the everyday reality of economic precarity sets back in. Our newly elected Democratic congressional leaders have an opportunity to change that reality — pushing back against Trump is necessary — but it cannot be the full extent of their ambition.

As a curator and the co-director of an arts nonprofit, I’ve been asked what the results mean for the so-called “art world.” My first response was cynical: “not much.” At least not immediately. An election does not directly restore a canceled grant or pay an artist’s rent. And even a return to the funding landscape that existed before Trump took office in 2025 would leave us with a system that was already failing the people expected to sustain it.

Instead, the midterm election results should serve as an opening to hold Democrats in Congress accountable for making arts and cultural life materially sustainable, not simply to defend an inadequate system from further attack. That mandate concerns whose histories are told, who gets paid to make art, and who gets to define the country’s future. It also concerns whether the people doing that work can afford to keep going.

#8967. How Frieze became the latest step in Abu Dhabi's cultural masterplan

Lighting up the city: the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi, which has taken over from the Abu Dhabi Art fair, is at the Manarat Al Saadiyat cultural hub on Saadiyat Island © Department of Culture and Tourism, Abu Dhabi

Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) debuts next week to a crescendo of cultural development in the emirate. As 2026 draws to a close it brings the launch of the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, which joins three other museums in the Saadiyat Cultural District that have opened in the past 18 months. Meanwhile, the second editions of the Public Art Biennial and Nomad Abu Dhabi art and design fair take place this month, while plans continue for Miza, the creative quarter in Mina Zayed.

While most of Abu Dhabi's cultural projects are newly launched, the city’s art fair has been running under various guises for nearly 20 years. It began in 2007 as ArtParis Abu Dhabi, held first at Emirates Palace, the luxury hotel on the Corniche, before later rebranding to Abu Dhabi Art and moving to Manarat Al Saadiyat, where it remains today. In those early years, galleries looked towards the newly announced Saadiyat museum projects. Heavyweights such as Gagosian, White Cube and Hauser & Wirth sold works primarily by Western artists at high prices and with institutional buyers in mind. As acquisition strategies shifted in the 2010s, many of the larger galleries left Abu Dhabi Art and the fair turned towards the Arab region and the Global South.

Frieze Abu Dhabi director Dyala Nusseibeh. “It’s a marriage,” Nusseibeh says about the fair’s partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism. “And the fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding” Courtesy Frieze Abu Dhabi

Regional stalwarts stayed, among them Green Art Gallery and the Third Line from Dubai, and Elmarsa from Tunisia, and it is thanks to the sustained efforts of the region's scene that art from the Arab world is gaining stature, institutional backing and international recognition. For example, the three artists on the stand of Dubai gallery Lawrie Shabibi—Mandy El-Sayegh, Shaikha Al Mazrou and Hamra Abbas—all now have international profiles. Meanwhile Dala Nasser, the inaugural winner of the Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, arrives fresh from solo shows at Nottingham Contemporary in the UK and Kunsthalle Basel in Switzerland.

This market, nonetheless, has conspicuously lagged. Art from the Arab world remains comparatively underexposed and relatively inexpensive. According to Dyala Nusseibeh, who joined Abu Dhabi Art as director in 2016 and now directs Frieze Abu Dhabi, the UAE accounted for 45% of all buyers of Mena (Middle East and North African) art in 2025. Collecting is rising among the younger Gulf generation, and the number of private collectors in Abu Dhabi has grown over the past decade, among Emiratis and foreign residents alike. Yet most Mena artists still sell to people with a connection to the region, a pattern both Frieze and the emirate are keen to break.

"We got to a point where we’d stretched as far as we could within our existing framework in building the market," Nusseibeh says. “We’re now ready for that next step outward—integrating the local and the regional market far better into the global market."

That step is a "marriage", Nusseibeh says, between the international fair giant and Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), which ran Abu Dhabi Art. “The fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding,” she says, framing the arrangement as an evolution of the fair rather than a takeover.

Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox describes the company following a growing market. “Our last new fair was in Seoul, and we just had our fifth edition, which was very successful,” he says. “We’ve been looking at how the art market is evolving, where collectors are, where there is growth. Unsurprisingly, this region is of great interest and becoming more so.”

Frieze’s offer is twofold. First, it promises greater international exposure for galleries and artists from the region, and not only through the curators and collectors it brings to Abu Dhabi. The Third Line, for example, secured a slot at No. 9 Cork Street—Frieze’s year-round London outpost—during Frieze London, on top of its place in Abu Dhabi. Second, the fair offers its regular Western galleries, facing a faltering market, entry to a new collecting cohort.

The Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, scheduled to open on 11 December, is in Abu Dhabi’s Saadiyat Cultural District Courtesy the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi

Despite Fox’s Seoul comparison, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents a different arrangement: it is a partnership with a state entity, behind which lies a web of capital and longstanding business relationships. Frieze was previously owned by Endeavor, the company run by Ari Emanuel. When Endeavor was taken private by the investment firm Silver Lake and its assets bought back in 2025, it was split into three: what Fox calls the “fighting assets”, the Ultimate Fighting Champion (UFC) and World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE), combined as TKO; the talent agency William Morris Endeavor (WME); and the live-events businesses, Frieze among them, under a new company founded by Emanuel called Mari.

Mubadala, one of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth funds, is a key backer of Silver Lake, having put in $2bn in 2020 and signed a 25-year strategic co-operation agreement. Mubadala has also invested directly in Mari, as has the Abu Dhabi media group IMI. That builds on a close relationship dating to the 2010s between Emanuel and Mubadala chief executive Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the brother of DCT director-general Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak.

This multifold investment by Abu Dhabi into Frieze should mean the fair is well supported, even as its first edition takes place amid regional instability. It should also ensure Frieze's plans align closely with those for the emirate as a whole. Nonetheless, the decision to not align the opening of Guggenheim Abu Dhabi with the fair will likely mean fewer international visitors for Frieze.

Zayed National Museum opened in December 2025 Courtesy Zayed National Museum

The arrival of Frieze, and the rest of Emanuel's portfolio, chimes with Abu Dhabi’s embrace of luxury and high-end events—which is, of course, another way to describe an art fair. Mari's holdings include elite tennis, such as the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open. The sovereign wealth fund ADQ’s $1bn investment in Sotheby’s in 2024 has produced a second year of auctions at the five-star St Regis hotel, where the auction house is selling jewellery as well as art. Next door to Manarat Al Saadiyat, the fair’s venue, sits not only the museums but the luxury Saadiyat Grove Mall, where its developer, Aldar, also chaired by Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, has commissioned major works by serious artists. Emanuel has often called this the entertainment and experience ecosystem: a synergistic portfolio spanning live events, luxury and leisure.

How measurably this will touch the fair itself remains to be seen. When Endeavor, then WME-IMG, took a stake in Frieze in 2016, pundits predicted crossovers between celebrities and artists that never materialised, and WME was later reconfigured as a separate entity. Frieze maintains that it retains full creative control, although with input from DCT, and has no plans to alter the art-centred formula that has served it well.

The luxury connection matters less for the fair than for what it reveals about Abu Dhabi’s positioning as a city for global elites. The private-equity and investment firms that have been arriving at pace until Iran's missile strikes on the Gulf earlier this year tell the same story. As does the commitment to an event-driven lifestyle, with calendar points throughout the year that drive business to the emirate. This week, Frieze; next month, the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Collectors’ Week and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.

Stepping back, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents one part of a longer, grander plan for the emirate. Accordingly, its success will be measured not only in sales, but whether the artists at its heart will eventually launch onto the global stage. The Guggenheim's arrival is expected to further propel Abu Dhabi's efforts to canonise not only the UAE’s contemporary scene, but also the history of Arab Modernism, which unfolded largely further west in the Maghreb, Egypt, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq.

The fair’s geography has also widened since its early editions, most notably with the growing importance of South Asian artists and collectors. Some of the most successful stands in recent years at Abu Dhabi Art have come from the subcontinent, and Frieze boasts a significant South Asian contingent, including Experimenter, Galerie Isa, Jhaveri Contemporary, Nature Morte and Project 88. South Asia shapes the non-commercial programme too: the curator Tarini Malik anchors her section, Global Futures, in the Arabian Sea, which connects South Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, and positions Abu Dhabi at the heart of a re-ordered world.

Taking over the longstanding Abu Dhabi Art, the Frieze brand has lured international dealerships alongside a strong showing of regional names

#8966. Cinga Samson "Ukuphuthelwa" @ White Cube Gallery, NYC

South African artist Cinga Samson’s exhibition of new paintings is titled ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, an isiXhosa word in the artist’s native language that translates as ‘unable to sleep’. Unlike the English word ‘insomnia’, the isiXhosa term carries no negative connotation and accordingly, for Samson, sleeplessness is not a condition to be cured but a state of spiritual alertness, a sensitivity that deepens in the dark. Rendered in the artist’s signature occluded palette of near-blacks, carbon and deep Prussian blues, Samson’s scenes depict men-like figures, dogs in overgrown fields and portraits of plant life native to South Africa. Encouraging slow, contemplative looking, a sense of existential gravity pervades Samson’s new series of oil paintings, attempting to depict a vast reality that is continuously in motion. As the artist has it, his quandary pertains to the existential question of how to create a ‘true and honest painting'. The exhibition will be on view through April 18, 2026.

With ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, Samson considers his role as an artist in relation to his inability to represent the whole truth of reality, and the fact that he can merely make symbols. Between the static, painted sign and the fluid experience it gestures towards, he contends that there exists a gulf that no image can close. Though the technical mastery and convincing realism of these paintings appear to invite interpretation, the artist asserts that his work confronts the very dilemma of representation: that the image can only ever be a relative symbol of what it reflects, never its equivalent. Acknowledging the open-ended nature of symbols and their subjective interpretation, Samson takes the figure of the dog as an example. The viewer may, for instance, look at Intsingiselo II (2026) and perceive the loyalty conventionally associated with dogs, while an amaXhosa understanding might highlight the dog as signifying the guiding, protective principles of ancestors. Comprising painstaking detail and deft brushwork, Samson’s paintings do not disguise the limits of representation but, rather, aspire to harness his skills towards that which exceeds the representable. Above all, the artist’s work seeks out the authority of the unnameable and the territory of the sublime, one in which the divine is not found elsewhere but present in the vernacular of all things.

Samson’s larger compositions carry a palpable sense of reverence and ceremony. In Umlindo (Watcher) (2026), figures are gathered in a forest clearing with wildflower bouquets and lengths of fabric, a scene that carries the visual grammar of ritual without specifying its addressee or terms. For Samson however, ‘the ritual itself is not the important thing – it’s an opening to what exists beyond’, and the paintings use the aesthetics of ritual to speak to a collective need for orientation, as well as the capacity of ritual to mediate an encounter with a vast unknown. That the works are titled with enigmatic words and phrases in isiXhosa, such as Imfihlo (Secret) and Intsingiselo (Meaning) (both 2026), infer the same problem the paintings contend with – the instability of interpretation as it pertains to the knowable and unknowable. Each word carries a weight in isiXhosa that its English translation approaches but can never fully reach; here, just as between the painted sign and living referent, meaning slips between the interstice of two languages.

The objects, people and settings that recur in these paintings and across Samson’s oeuvre are identifiable and quotidian, yet Samson corrals in each an unexplained mystery. In Tshee (2026), a vast field stretches out, the silhouetted trees meeting a murky sky, though the void of the night is interrupted by a moonwashed cloud, its brilliant white destabilising the eerie, cold atmosphere suffused with majesty. ‘The sky can be so friendly, but sometimes so heavy, dark, so scary. It’s the same energy, but it exists in different forms’, Samson notes, conjuring an oscillation between the approachable and the overwhelming that recalls the affective register of the sublime. Sithini ngelilitye (2026), distils the same sensation: a rocky crag emerges from arid undergrowth, its surface rendered in forensic detail against a sky of barely-there wash, charging the scene with the same quality of mute enormity.

Marshalling light ‘like a magic trick’, Samson imparts a unique kind of rhythm to his paintings – a flickering that emerges and disperses across the picture plane, granting varying degrees of visibility to the dark, nighttime scenes. Producing an unsteadiness that is at once optical and psychical, the artist leaves large sections of the painting’s under-drawing visible to lend moments of transparency to the work. In Isiganeko (2026), for example, thin layers of glaze are applied and wiped back in his typical style, a means of building colour that lends the figures a brooding chromatic density, whilst elsewhere, in the undergrowth and the bird caught mid-flight, the under-drawing is left entirely exposed. In all Samson’s figures, the pupils of the eyes are left unpainted and allow ‘light’ to further circulate, a decision that renders them porous, so they are ‘completely one with the whole painting’. Without pupils, these figures are not personified identities, but ‘human’ forms enmeshed with the painting’s landscape and atmosphere, no element ever possessing full mastery over the other. In places where the ‘trick’ of painting reveals itself, it is as if Samson’s works were stepping back from the pretence or promise of representation. What ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ reaches towards is not individual transcendence in subordination, but rather the mystery that can be unearthed in ordinary forms, whose immanent magic is available to those who are sensitive to it. This is the condition that ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ ultimately describes: not an absence or deficit, but a hypersensitivity that affords everything in existence the same potential for eliciting wonder or fear. Samson’s pupilless figures do not ‘look’ outward because the figures’ knowing comes from within the world they inhabit, a shared knowledge that exists between the bowing foliage, the vigilant dog, the bird in flight and the foreboding of the night sky enshrouding them all. In Samson’s hands, each optical device and representational motif prises apart what it cannot contain, in service of painting ‘a thing that links us to God – by God, I mean everything’.

#8965. The Art World's Neoliberal Capture

In “The Battleground of Art,” curator and activist Marco Baravalle dissects the art establishment's co-optation of radical politics and uplifts the stories of collectives that resist it.

We first met Marco Baravalle in 2015 at the 56th Venice Biennale, All the World’s Futures, when we were organizing with the Gulf Labor Coalition. The group and our autonomous direct-action wing, Global Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.), had been invited by curator Okwui Enwezor to present our research and organizing against migrant worker exploitation in the construction of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. An artist boycott was underway, direct actions were escalating, and days earlier, on May 1, we had shut down the Guggenheim Museum in New York City.

Through Baravalle, a longtime researcher, curator, and activist, we encountered a network of autonomous spaces in Venice and Milan. These were not simply cultural centers; they formed the infrastructure for collective organizing, resistance, and enacting other worlds.

Eleven years later, The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism (2026) extends this praxis into an important and timely call to action. Drawing on his two decades of experience, Baravalle offers what we have called movement-generated theory and practice, rooted in the dialectic of doing and knowing. The book confronts the neoliberal capture of the art world, while also excavating histories and practices of abolition and autonomy that offer other possibilities.

#8964. Sophia Huitema "Prussian Blue" @ Harper’s Apartment

Harper’s is pleased to announce Prussian Blue, New York–based artist Sophia Huitema’s first solo exhibition with the gallery. The presentation features new works by Huitema and will be on view through April 25, 2026.

Across the seven oil paintings on view, the visual and chemical properties of the pigment Prussian Blue function as a metaphorical anchor, tying together a cast of watchful female figures within Huitema’s hazy, dreamlike worlds. Working within a restrained range of blue and green tones, the paintings evoke a moody atmosphere through cool harmonies and dimly lit interiors. Prussian Blue, derived from chemical processes historically linked to cyanide while also used as an antidote to certain forms of poisoning, embodies a rare duality in which toxicity and protection converge, mirroring the emotionally guarded, ambiguous presence of Huitema’s figures.

The tension between beauty and menace permeates Huitema’s subjects. Elongated figures with exaggerated limbs and slender necks slink through each scene, often directly confronting the viewer’s gaze. Set within opulent surroundings that recall Gatsby–era decadence, Huitema’s women bear the markers of high society themselves, dressed in elegant gowns and adorned with pearl necklaces or jewel-studded headdresses. Moving through film-noir settings with poise and a quietly calculating air, these femme fatales seem either to lure their audience into a seductive ruse or to deploy their own cunning to evade danger. In Sleeper Car, for example, a woman fitted in a backless evening gown tilts her head slyly over her right shoulder in a relaxed pose while her right hand appears braced and ready to strike. As rain streaks across the coach’s windows and the narrow aisle stretches into an uncertain depth, a moment of cinematic suspense emerges, evoking the apex of a psychological thriller. In this way, Huitema constructs a world of heightened atmosphere and theatrical tension that opens onto the broader visual traditions and painterly languages informing her work.

Huitema’s paintings draw on a range of art-historical and visual references while maintaining a distinct internal coherence. The attenuated proportions and stylized poses of her figures recall traditions of early twentieth-century fashion illustration and Art Deco design, where gesture and embellishment echo the streamlined finesse of illustrators such as Erté and the theatrical poise found in interwar couture and stage design. Her compressed spaces also suggest affinities with aspects of Symbolist and Surrealist painting, in which shallow interiors and phantasmagoric backdrops function less as coherent environments than as psychological realms shaped by subconscious experience. Rather than aligning with a single historical framework, Huitema synthesizes these influences into a contemporary visual language that moves fluidly between illustration, painting, and cinematic staging. Working outside formal academic training, she has developed this vocabulary through sustained studio practice and close observation, resulting in a body of work that situates itself in dialogue with art history while remaining grounded in a self-directed approach to image making. In this context, Prussian Blue operates not only as a chromatic throughline but also as a conceptual one, binding together Huitema’s historical references and recurring motifs of protection and threat in constant tension.

After Jensen Huang’s resignation, maybe it's time for the company to finally rebrand.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Today, the Nvidia logo is recognised not only by dedicated gamers and creatives interested in the best graphics cards for video editing. The company's stock performance has turned it into a household name, while the demand for computer components amid the AI boom has ensured that a new headline is never far away.

Alas, it turns out that the DLSS 5 controversy is the least of its problems. Former CEO Jensen Huang has now resigned after embroiling Nvidia in a honeytrap scandal worthy of a spy novel. CFO Colette Kress has stepped up as interim CEO and an executive search has begun.

But the debacle has also resurfaced another question. Why does one of the world's most valuable companies still have such a terrible logo design? And could this be the moment for a refresh?

See our guides to the best laptops for graphic design and the best monitors for graphics artists if you need new tools for your own work.

Over on Reddit, designers are debating the "least aesthetically pleasing, most poorly designed corporate logo" still in use today, and the Nvidia logo is the example that was used to get the ball rolling. Other contenders put forward on the thread include the X logo and, of course, the infamous Kia logo.

I can see where the OP is coming from. Nvidia was the world's most valuable company until the Jensen Huang honeytrap controversy hammered its share price and put Apple back in the lead on the Nasdaq. The identities of those two companies couldn't look or feel more different. The Apple logo is sleek and minimalist. It feels modern and premium. The Nvidia logo is... weird.

"So many things I hate about this design: The Aztec-looking spiral eye, the half inverted color, the lime green, black, and white color pallette, the '80s sci-fi font. None of it coheres well," the OP writes on Reddit.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Of course, Apple and Nvidia are very different beasts. Apple is mainly consumer facing and Nvidia's business is mainly corporate. On the consumer side, Nvidia's GPUs are packaged and sold by other brands rather than by Nvidia directly. But the company is becoming much more of a household name as its tentacles spread.

Nvidia components are being promoted more visibly in GeForce RTX laptops, and the company's being collaborating on workflow developments with creative software developers like Adobe, Blackmagic (DaVinci Resolve) and the Blender Foundation.

There is a compelling case for a change. Nvidia's visual identity was born in a very different age of technology back in 1993. Its last logo redesign was twenty years ago in 2006.

Time alone is never a reason for a rebrand, even for a tech company. IBM's had the same logo since 1972. But with Nvidia, the age shows. The wonky eye, brat green colour palette and retro-futuristic type feel rooted in the late 1990s and early 2000s, when aggressive, futuristic aesthetics dominated PC hardware branding.

Compared with the cleaner, more restrained identities of companies like Apple, Microsoft, OpenAI and even AMD, Nvidia's main rival in the GPU space, the branding feels tied to gaming origins.

There's also a somewhat dark occult reference going on. In the company's name, the 'NV' comes from the shorthand that was used to identify the 'next version' in file names, while the 'invidia' part means 'envy' in Latin.

That feeling will be familiar to anyone who has a colleague with an RTX 5090, but it's a strange choice for a brand. The word is often associated with malice and the 'evil eye' and was sometimes used as the Roman name for the ancient Greek deity, Nemesis, the personification of divine retribution. Yikes.

Today, the firm's influence and ambitions extend far beyond GeForce. It sells AI infrastructure, networking technology, autonomous vehicle platforms and enterprise computing systems. A more refined visual identity could reflect its status as a global AI platform rather than a 'mere' component manufacturer.

That said, for all of its weirdness, Nvidia's mysterious green eye is one of the most distinctive marks in tech. A rebrand could risk of abandoning something that has aged better than critics might admit.

While the eye doesn't feel especially contemporary, it is unique. At a time when many companies are converging towards minimalist sans-serif wordmarks and simplified geometric symbols, the identity stands out precisely because it has character, and distinctiveness is arguably more valuable than modernity.

The strongest argument would probably be for a careful evolution. The company could modernise the typography and tweak the eye. It might be able to find a more appealing shade of green. A relatively subtle refresh could preserve decades of recognition while signalling that Nvidia has entered a new chapter.

But it remains to be seen how much the last two weeks have changed things. It looked like Jensen Huang was going to hang on until yesterday's resignation announcement. The company might also decide that the controversy requires a clear visual break from the past.

There's plenty of branding inspiration about this week that Nvidia might want to check out, from the solid Caixa rebrand in Brazil to the intriguing new Takara Tomy logo .

Let me know below if you agree that Nvidia has the worst corporate logo in tech, or if you feel that there's a stronger candidate.
