How do you make a branching game feel like a TV show? AdHoc’s co-founders explain, from recording Aaron Paul’s cast in conversation to ditching Telltale’s habits.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dispatch looks, sounds, and plays like an animated TV show, and that was deliberate: AdHoc wanted it to be a no-barrier entry point for people who don't usually play games. A year after its launch on 22 October 2025, the episodic superhero workplace comedy has more than five million players, and the new Dispatch Deluxe Edition offers new ways to play, including replacing its graphics with storyboard art.

The game stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as Robert Robertson, a former hero turned dispatcher for a team of reformed supervillains, alongside Jeffrey Wright, Laura Bailey, and members of the Critical Role cast. Getting that cast to feel like they're in the same room, and getting the player to feel part of the story, took a lot of invisible work.

You can read how four video tracks and a doughnut shop gave Dispatch its start, but here I ask co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO, and both co-creative directors, how they nailed down the premium animation.

How do you keep dialogue, facial expressions and performances consistent when the player can send a scene in different directions? While it was made using Unreal Engine 5, it starts on the page. "Everything is written with choice in mind," says Herman.

AdHoc built its own tools to ingest scripts, including a playable script you can read and click through. That produces the recording script actors use in the booth, which Herman says is "a little bit crazy to read on a linear page". Do it long enough, though, and it starts to make sense. Each scene has a spine, and every time a choice appears, different options eventually trunk back into the main flow.

The studio also uses recordings as a directing tool. AdHoc ingests every performance as it’s captured, so when an actor records opposite someone already in the booth, the team can play those existing lines back for them to react to. In Herman’s example, with Aaron Paul already recorded, the team can bring in Erin as Blonde Blazer, play Paul’s lines for her to read off, then play him again after her response. It’s a clever bit of craft: AdHoc builds each conversation around real delivery. The effect, Herman says, is to simulate the actors being in the same room, which helps performances feel grounded and integrated. It also gives a scene its flow, because the actors know where they’re coming in from, and it makes testing branches easy.

It's clever craft. Rather than recording actors in isolation and hoping the performances fit together later, AdHoc builds the conversation around real delivery. The effect, Herman says, is to simulate the actors being in the same room, which helps performances feel grounded and integrated. It also gives a scene its flow, because the actors know where they're coming in from, and it makes testing branches easy.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

By the time animation begins, the voice work is trusted, and the team is happy with it. The facial animation then comes down to knowing every character. "Not everyone laughs the same. When they cry, they look different," Herman says. "Every character is their own person. Like they are on the page, they are in animation." Getting there takes "a lot of review, a lot of ref", and the team shoots plenty of reference footage for its animators.

For AdHoc, the problem was the seam: the point where a cutscene ends and gameplay begins. “The goal was always to make it feel integrated,” Lenart says. Part of the studio’s philosophy is that gameplay and story should feel like a seamless handoff rather than two different experiences. He and Herman had worked on plenty of games with clear story sections and clear gameplay sections, “and you could feel that break every single time”. That, he says, “always kind of drove us crazy”.

When they dreamed of starting their own studio, one mandate was to choose mechanics that feel like an integrated part of a character's life, not scenes contrived for interactivity. If someone has to break into a room and pick a lock, it shouldn't be something the character would never do.

For Dispatch, that meant the shift mechanic. Robert sends heroes out on calls because it's his job. "It's the thing he does every day," says Lenart. "So, when he sits down at his computer to do it, it feels natural."

The team also made sure the Z-Team keep talking to the player throughout each shift, so the dialogue and relationships keep flowing, and the story never stops for gameplay. At times, a shift cuts out to a cinematic and back in again, and Lenart says that only feels organic because "we spent a lot of time and effort to make it that way".

Herman and Lenart both spent years at Telltale Games, the studio behind The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, and Tales from the Borderlands, and Dispatch forced them to drop much of their old way of working.

At Telltale, Lenart says, cinematics were "fast and loose". Episodes were made in what the studio called live development: they would release one episode, then spend the next six weeks on the following. Things "could change at any time". Player feedback from the previous episode could feed straight back in, with tweaks to cinematics and character intentions right up until the day before shipping.

Dispatch had a different goal. AdHoc wanted the visuals and style to feel like "a premium animated television show" that wasn't a barrier for people who might enjoy a story like this but aren't typically into games. That meant a more traditional animation pipeline, with decisions made much earlier and, in some cases, locked down a year in advance.

"That was a really big learning curve for us since we were used to being able to make small adjustments all the way up until the last minute," Lenart says. But he now thinks the discipline made the game better. It "forced many detailed conversations way earlier in the process, which only better informed how each piece of the story was going to play out". His verdict: "Oh, this is actually the way to make the best quality product."

The Dispatch Deluxe Edition is out now on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and Nintendo Switch / Switch 2, and $10.99 digital upgrade path for existing owners

#8895. ARTnews Awards 2026 Historical Artist of the Year: Theresa Hak Kyung Cha

Honoring a deceased artist who is the subject of a major museum survey that offers a new lens with which to examine their work.

Theresa Hak Kyung Chafor “Theresa Hak Kyung Cha: Multiple Offerings” at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (January 24–April 19, 2026); traveled to Artists Space, New York (September 11–November 21, 2026)Curators: Victoria Sung, with Tausif Noor

Since her untimely death in 1982, Theresa Hak Kyung Cha has been a touchstone for academics and artists alike. Best known for Dictée, a genre-defying book that combines fiction, memoir, hagiography, and more, Cha was this year the subject of a BAMPFA retrospective that offered a new lens from which to view the artist’s practice. It expanded the scope beyond Dictée and brought together early ceramics, documentation of her performances, text-based works, mail art, and video art, all of which was elegantly installed. Related Articles ARTnews Awards 2026 Established Artist of the Year: Vaginal Davis ARTnews Awards 2026 Lifetime Achievement: Maren Hassinger

Cha’s experience of moving to the United States from Korea during her childhood animated her practice, giving her fertile ground to think through what it means to live in diaspora and be caught between two cultures. In this space, where words might fail to fully explain one’s experience, she found a place to make art. The exhibition’s title “Multiple Offerings” borrows its names from the phrase “Multiple Telling with Multiple Offerings,” a conceptual framework that guided Cha’s art-making, resulting in works that were not meant to be experienced in just one way. Instead of giving easy answers, or even a single answer, Cha’s practice starts a conversation. We are left to pick up the pieces and make meaning from them.

Curator Victoria Sung traced the important moments of Cha’s short yet productive career, focusing on the decade she spent as a student at the University of California, Berkeley, which houses BAMPFA, and periods spent in New York, France, and South Korea. At the time of her death, Cha was at work on a major film, White Dust From Mongolia, that she was never able to fully realize, despite having produced storyboards and shot footage for the work. Artists like Na Mira and Cici Wu have looked to White Dust From Mongolia and created work in response to it; those pieces were included in the BAMPFA exhibition. With their inclusion, Sung also made the case for Cha as an artist whose influence has recently come into focus.

#8894. ZAV Architects extends house in Iran with ombre "architectural limbs"

Photography by Parham Taghioff unless otherwise stated

A series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue on this home extension on the outskirts of Tehran, designed by Iranian studio ZAV Architects.

Named Golmorad, the colourful extension transforms the residence from a weekend villa, originally designed by Iranian studio Firouz Firouz, into a permanent home in the town of Kouhsar.

ZAV Architects‘ intervention extends both ends of the home into three adjacent orchard plots acquired by the client.

Constructed from masonry, the extension is coated in plaster to blend in with the earthen exterior of the original home, while its curved geometries set it apart from its predecessor.

Aiming to appear as if organically growing from the home, Golmorad emerges as a series of overlapping arched roofs.

At one end, the vaulted extension branches into two curved forms that gradually decrease in height – one wing containing a bedroom and ensuite, and the other an open-plan kitchen, living and dining room that opens onto an outdoor pool.

Openings between the overlapping roof planes let light into the home’s interior.

“Rather than approaching the extension as either a replication of the original structure or a distinctly separate addition, the project explores a third possibility: an architecture that emerges from within the existing building itself,” ZAV Architects told Dezeen.

“This intervention can be understood as a process of grafting, in which new needs and aspirations are grafted onto the existing body of the villa, giving rise to new architectural limbs that branch out and grow from it,” it continued.

“It is as though the original building, while retaining its underlying architectural logic rooted in thick-earth construction, has developed new and distinct organs of its own.”

ZAV Architects created a gradient effect across the building with terracotta tones fading into blue, intending to strengthen the appearance of the extension growing from the home.

“The uniform colour of the original villa develops into a chromatic spectrum that radiates outward from the existing core towards the newly formed branches,” the studio said.

“This transition makes the process of transformation visible, with each segmented shell expressing a distinct stage in the building’s evolution.”

Golmorad is shortlisted in the house extension category of this year’s Dezeen Awards. It recently won the awards’ public vote alongside a playground also designed by ZAV Architects.

Last year, ZAV Architects was among the winners of the Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the Majara Residence and Community Redevelopment, a colourful domed cultural retreat on the Iranian island of Hormuz.

#8893. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

#8892. ARTnews Awards 2026 Emerging Artist of the Year: Coco Klockner

Recognizing an artist who is having their first significant gallery or small nonprofit solo show or has made an important contribution to a biennial.

Coco Klocknerfor “In Practice: Coco Klockner” at SculptureCenter, New York (October 18, 2025–December 22, 2025) and her contribution to “Greater New York 2026” at MoMA PS1, New York (April 16–August 17, 2026)

Coco Klockner has said she approaches making sculpture “as though it were in transition,” a turn of phrase that refers to the unknowable, shape-shifting quality that has characterized much of her work since her first gallery show in 2018. At New York’s SculptureCenter, she continued that line of thinking with her “In Practice” exhibition, which was largely composed of one ambitious installation: null dialogue (2025), a work that was composed of subwoofers, construction fill, and an amplifier, among other materials. An easily missed motion detector at the entrance set off the piece’s soundtrack, which Klockner has described as “an undisclosed conversation between lovers.” Yet the words of that conversation were heavily edited and therefore difficult to understand, and the show itself contained little information about the work. A machine emitted fog every three minutes, cloaking the space in a mysterious haze. Depending on when one encountered Klockner’s SculptureCenter show, null dialogue may have been heard before it was seen. Indeed, Klockner has described drawing influence from the notion of thinking of “sounds as objects.” Related Articles ARTnews Awards 2026 Established Artist of the Year: Vaginal Davis ARTnews Awards 2026 Lifetime Achievement: Maren Hassinger

She gave that idea new form with her contribution to MoMA PS1’s 2026 edition of Greater New York, where she showed Glottoplasty (2026), an installation in which plastic storage drawers embedded with speakers play sliced and sutured excerpts from trans oral archives. As with null dialogue, the words emitted were nearly impossible to parse, even if they were played quite loudly. The work suggested an effort to simultaneously reveal and conceal. Implicit in both the SculptureCenter show and the PS1 work was an interest in the body. Glottoplasty took its name from a medical procedure that is used to raise the pitch of one’s voice; null dialogue was accompanied by an untitled work composed of a plastic mouth retractor, wood filler, and 935 silver. Notably, at both presentations, it was possible to feel the rumbling of Klockner’s art while standing before it.

#8891. Viking legend informs ring-like viewpoint on Icelandic mountain ridge

Photography by Claudio Parada Nunes

Ring of Bjólfur is a mountain viewpoint in Iceland, designed by local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking.

Located in Seyðisfjörður, a fjord in eastern Iceland, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture‘s design draws on the legend of Bjólfur, an Icelandic Viking settler believed to have claimed this landscape and been laid to rest on the mountain.

Local lore says Bjólfur was buried on the mountain with his most precious belongings, though they have never been found. The viewpoint, therefore, evokes a ring that has been left for him.

“The medieval Book of Settlements, or Landnámabók, tells of Bjólfur, the settler who first claimed land in Seyðisfjörður and gave the mountain its name,” Arkibygg Architects told Dezeen.

“The book says little about him, but local tales tell that he was laid to rest in a burial mound high up on the mountain,” it continued.

“By ancient custom, chieftains were often buried with their treasures, silver and jewellery. Bjólfur’s grave goods have never been found, but we let our imagination run free and left him a great silver ring.”

Arkibygg Arkitektar and Esja Architecture won a competition to design Ring of Bjólfur in 2021. The project was shortlisted in the small projects category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and also won the public vote for the same category.

Ring of Bjólfur takes the form of a perfect circle, measuring 32 metres in diameter. While emulating a ring, this was also designed to “work with views in every direction”.

Positioned on a mountain ridge 650 metres above sea level, the structure was built from post-tensioned concrete with stainless steel railings, chosen for durability and for colours that emulate silver. It partially cantilevers on one side.

“The ring can be used in many ways, and the view changes depending on where you are in the circle – and whether you are standing or sitting,” said Arkibygg Arkitektar.

“The choice of materials grew from the idea of creating a silver ring, while also having to withstand wind and weather at 650 metres, with the structure being submerged in snow for parts of the year,” said the studio.

A major focus for the studios was ensuring accessibility, creating “an experience that everyone can enjoy, including wheelchair users”.

To achieve this, they designed accessible parking next to the ring as part of the project. Further general parking is located further downhill to encourage people who are physically able to walk to the platform.

“The project has been very well received, not only by visitors but just as much by local residents,” it continued.

“The ring is already strengthening tourism in the town, and it has also become part of residents’ daily lives, widely used for outdoor recreation. People walk, cycle or even ski up there to take in the view.”

The landscape surrounding the viewpoint was preserved as much as possible, with any boulders that needed to be temporarily removed lifted back into place upon completion.

“The immediate surroundings – the soil and the rocks – matter a great deal. The aim was to disturb the ground as little as possible and to repair what was disturbed.

“Other areas affected by the works were restored with native vegetation. Having one clear destination also keeps visitors from wandering across the fragile ridge.”

Other viewpoints recently featured on Dezeen include an arrow-shaped structure in Denmark by Arup and the Lech Mountain Mirror by Snøhetta in Austria.

Black Friday iPad deals are already coming in, with early discounts on most models as the holidays approach. But, having tracked iPad Black Friday prices for close to a decade, I'd hold off buying for now in all but one case: Amazon's $100 off the M4 iPad Air.

With iPad prices inevitably more expensive than during Black Friday last year because of RAM and SSD shortages, this could be as good a deal as we get on the latest Air, and it offers pretty good value. If you do need more power, up to $150 off the M5 iPad Pro at B&H Photo is also tempting. But I think the lower-spec iPads could still fall in price as Black Friday gets closer.

If you need help deciding which iPad to choose, our expert guides to the iPad generations and the best iPad for drawing are the places to turn to.

This is a decent if not spectacular deal on the starting configuration of the 11-inch model. B&H also has $100 off the larger 13-inch iPad Pro which we gave 4.5 stars in our review when we recently tested it, and up to $150 off the 512GB SSD configuration of that tablet.

This is the iPad to go for if you're looking for a potential laptop replacement capable of video editing and heavy graphics work on the go. It has the best display on an iPad, with the OLED screen providing up to 1600 nits peak brightness for HDR work and a fast 120Hz refresh rate for zero lag.

The M4 iPad Air was only released in March of this year, so $100 off might be the best deal we see over Black Friday 2026, and it's not to be sniffed at. This is the iPad we recommend for most people as t's significantly more affordable than the pro, but still has Apple Pencil Pro support and enough power for digital drawing, photo editing and light video editing in Final Cut. There's also $100 off its larger 13-inch sibling.

The latest generation of the basic iPad is a good a choice as ever for anyone looking for a general, everyday tablet for browsing, entertainment and casual sketching and notetaking. This tablet was also released in March 2025, and Amazon had $70 off the original price during Black Friday last year, so this deal could (I would say should) get better.

A new iPad mini was released just this month with the faster A20 Pro chip. We've not seen any discounts on that yet, and its starting price is $100 more than that of its predecessor at $699. That makes a $130 difference when you consider this discount at Amazon.

In that context, the 2024 model is still worth considering if you're looking for a creative powerhouse in a very small package. It's more powerful than the standard iPad above and support Apple Pencil Pro, making it a small but mighty option for sketching and notetaking on the go.

iPad Black Friday deals in the UK aren't great so far, but any saving is welcome on Apple's best tablet – we've not seen any discount at all since Apple hiked prices in April because of the RAM crisis.

Very has a small saving on the latest generation of the basic iPad, which we rated as a decent upgrade from its predecessor when we tested it earlier this year. This is one deal I would hope to see improved on as we get closer to Black Friday proper, but given high price of tech at the moment, who knows?

Compatible with the 2024 and 2025 iPad Pros and iPad Airs as well as the latest iPad mini, the Pencil Pro is Apple's most sophisticated iPad stylus, with haptic feedback, a pinch gesture to control actions and a barrel roll feature to change brushes. This fell as cheap as $89 during Black Friday last year, but 2025 prices feel like a long, long time ago today.

This is actually a really good deal on Apple's best inner-ear headphones yet. Released a year ago, they have improved Active Noise Cancellation and battery life compared to the previous gen AirPods Pro, as well as a better fit, improved water and dust resistance and a new heart rate sensor.

This the lowest price we've seen for a keyboard case that does two jobs in one, protecting your iPad (it's compatible with the latest 10in iPad) while also adding keyboard functionality, making the tablet convenient for work and email. We find Logitech's officially endorsed options are sleek and well built, and this is a very good saving.

Apple hiked the price of all of its current iPad models around the middle of 2026 because of the increase in the cost of components, particularly memory (RAM) and internal storage (SSDs). The whole consumer tech sector has been impacted by these price rises, which have been caused by a shortage of component due to the demand from companies building AI data centres.

This means that this year's iPad Black Friday deals will inevitably be more expensive than last year's. There's no sign that starting prices will fall again any time soon.

Keeping in mind the size of discounts seen during previous iPad Black Friday sales is a good way to gauge whether it's the right time to buy or if prices could fall further. The pattern we've seen is that the best deals on the latest generation of iPads tend to be up to $70 off the standard iPad and $100 off the iPad Air and up to $200 off higher-spec iPad Pros.

In 14 years of tracking prices, our experience is that there is rarely any difference between Black Friday and Cyber Monday iPad prices. They are usually the same deals under a different name. On a very few occasions, we have seen new discounts appear on Cyber Monday.

The best iPad for you will depend on what you want to use it for. For browsing, watching movies, social media and just occasional note taking and sketching, this year's standard 11-inch iPad with the A16 chip will do just fine, and it doesn't make sense to spend more. Aim to spend no more than $399 on this,

If you're an artist and want a more efficient drawing experience, I'd recommend stepping up to the iPad Air. A new M4-chipped generation of this tablet was released in March, and Amazon's already slashed the price by $100 in a Black Friday deal. This tablet comes in two choices of size: 11 inches or 13 inches.

If you're a professional artist and you have the budget for it, the iPad Pro is the top-of-the-range option. Also coming in 11- and 13-inch models, it has a superior screen with a bright OLED panel for improved contrast along along with a faster 120Hz refresh rate for a seamless drawing experience.

Coming with the M5 chip, this is the iPad to choose if you want to replace you're laptop when working on the go, and it's cut out to handle more demanding creative software, including video editing.

Remember that all iPads come in various configurations, with the option of WiFi and cellular connectivity or just WiFi alone, plus two size options for the Pro and Air and at least two choices of internal storage capacity. When quoting prices above, we've generally quoted the price of the base model with WiFi and the smallest SSD. This might not necessarily be the option that meets your needs, but retailers will usually list other configurations under the same product listing.

If you use a tablet for work and want to store large files on the device, you may need a higher capacity. The iPad Pro, for example, is available with 256GB, 512GB, 1TB or 2TB. the price rises notably, but the higher-spec models sometimes come in for bigger discounts.

We'll be linking directly to the best Black Friday iPad deals across all four models here on this page. The best thing you can do to prepare to choose the best deal for you is to think ahead about which iPad you want and in which configuration.

Once you've decided which iPad you want (the Pro, Air, mini or standard iPad), choose the size (there's a choice of 11in or 13in with the iPad Pro and iPad Air), whether you want cellular connectivity or WiFi alone and which storage capacity you'll think you need. Whether you can make do with the starting capacity or you need to hike it up to 512GB, or even 1TB or 2TB on the iPad Pro will depend on how you expect to use the device and whether you'll also be using cloud storage or will want to store large design or video files on the tablet itself.

Apple is unlikely to run any direct iPad Black Friday discounts itself. Instead, it's likely yo offer gift vouchers worth up to $100/£80 with the purchase of certain iPads. This might be appealing if you know that you're going to want to buy another Apple product in the future, but most people would be better off going for deals at third-party sites.

In previous years, we have seen good Black Friday iPad deals at most of the major retailers in the US and UK. In the US, Amazon and B&H Photo tend to have the best prices, while Walmart and Target can also be worth checking.

In the UK, Amazon and Very tend to have the biggest discounts, while Laptops Direct is worth checking for discounts on older models. We track prices at all of these retailers and more.

Traditionally, Black Friday was the Friday after Thanksgiving in the US. It's since extended to cover almost all of November at some retailers. As for when Black Friday ends, many retailers continue it until the Monday after Black Friday itself, which some call Cyber Monday. This year, that falls on 30 November 2026.

#8889. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

#8888. Mori AI home robot "resembles a contemporary table lamp"

Robotics startup OKA has released a lamp-shaped artificial intelligence robot designed to offer companionship by greeting people, dancing to music and playing nature sounds.

Mori by OKA (One Kind Artificat) is 26.4 centimetres tall, with a cloth-covered base and an illuminated, dome-shaped head that lifts to reveal cartoonish eyes that blink and swivel.

According to OKA, Mori “resembles a contemporary table lamp” and was designed to “help people feel calmer, more at ease, and more connected to the world around them”.

“We wanted Mori to feel like a familiar object in the home rather than an unfamiliar machine,” OKA told Dezeen. “Many robots look technical, mechanical, or overly human, while a lamp is something people already live with comfortably.”

The robot exists in two modes: a lamp setting, when it’s compact and at rest, and a responsive setting, when the head is lifted and tilted.

Powered by the start-up’s proprietary AI system, the robot’s responses include playing audio informed by rain and other nature sounds, changing the colour of its lamp top and performing nonverbal communication through multi-axis neck and body movement.

Users tap the top of Mori’s head and it “retracts its face and becomes a quiet lamp”. As another part of its calming offerings, grabbing its base triggers a breathing exercise.

It also makes small sounds as part of these interactions.

“Mori’s soft silhouette and tactile materials let it blend into domestic interiors,” said OKA. “Its warmth, brightness, and subtle changes can suggest comfort, curiosity, or calm, which lets Mori express itself through illumination, sound, and movement instead of screens or conversation.”

According to the company, Mori will remember occupants, routines, and interaction history and adjust its behaviour accordingly, such as using “judgment to decide when to proactively engage or remain quiet”.

The AI model is based on the concept of Attentive Intelligence, built upon research by OKA co-founder Weizhe Chen. Attentive Intelligence is an emerging framework within AI, wherein a model is proactive versus reactive to prompts.

“It reads the room before responding and weighs whether to join in, so sometimes a small nod is enough and sometimes it stays quiet,” said OKA.

“Its responses are shaped by VIBE (Vitality, Interaction, Bonding, Emotion), an inner state that drifts with time and experience, so the same greeting can come out lively one day and gentle the next.”Mori comes in a variety of soft colourways and is rechargeable with a 2.5-hour battery life. However, OKA suggests keeping it plugged in.

OKA was founded in 2024 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, by entrepreneur and designer Hua Wang and robotics researcher Weizhe Che. The company is focused on creating robotic projects that “integrate seamlessly into human life rather than forcing human life to adapt to technology”.

OKA plans to release five major “artifacts” or products in its lifetime, according to the team. The Mori robot is the first.

Mori joins a growing number of home robots released recently with “embodied AI” – or the act of inserting an AI model into a robotic body.

Other home robots include the Droxel “droid butler” and Neo, a humanoid robot dressed in a cloth bodysuit.

#8887. Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home.

Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up!

Why are my ears clogged?

Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked:

  • Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage.
  • If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection.
  • Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side.
  • Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too.
  • Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure.

Best clogged ear remedies

1. Pop and unclog

The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes.

2. Swallow, yawn, or chew

The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow.

3. Ear drops

Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes.

Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful.

4. Warmth and gravity

To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

5. Hit the steam room

Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 

6. Take allergy medication

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

7. Rinse away the gunk

Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

When to see your doctor

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

What not to do when you have clogged ears

  • Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. 
  • Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries.
  • Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion.
  • Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation.

Takeaway

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

#8886. PPAA creates twin houses in Mexico as an "argument for building less"

Mexican architecture studio Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados has completed twin houses that combine concrete with glued-laminated timber in the forests of Valle de Bravo, Mexico.

The two houses – each measuring 500 square metres (5,382 square feet) – are collectively called Rejas and were designed for two brothers and their families, cohabitating on a 1.2-acre forested property in Avándaro, a couple of hours west of Mexico City.

“Avándaro is a landscape that’s been quietly overbuilt for decades, so the first decision on Rejas was actually a renunciation,” Pablo Pérez Palacios, founder of Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados (PPAA), told Dezeen,

“Instead of designing a wall or a fence between the two brothers’ houses, we chose to regenerate the native forest that the site had partially lost, and let that stand as the boundary,” he said, explainging that decision set the tone for the rest of the project.

“The whole project is really an argument for building less, so the landscape has room to eventually reclaim the architecture.”

The site, with its regenerated forest, is steeply sloped toward the Avándaro reservoir, allowing PPAA to partially submerge each house.

From the driveway, the houses appear as one-storey structures, but the lower levels emerge on the other side as the terrain descends.

To navigate this, the houses sit on bases of concrete and local stone that anchor them into the slope, while timber roofs top the upper levels and open the spaces to the surrounding trees.

The houses were designed to interact with the landscape, and have almost identical plans, though their place in the landscape differs.

Public spaces are on the upper level, with a kitchen, dining and living room in a glass box within the larger, rectangular platform.

A covered terrace comprises the remainder of the level with designated seating and outdoor cooking areas that are framed with planters.

Below, five bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms and a lounge area sit within the forest floor, cool and contained within the boxy volume.

“The deliberate positioning of the openings eliminates any possibility of facing windows – no window in one house looks toward the other. Each dwelling establishes its own relationship with the natural surroundings as if the other did not exist.”

The studio pulled the service areas for both houses into separate buildings placed along the edge of the property to free the centre of the plot for the houses and their relationships with the landscape.

Designed to patina with the landscape, the minimalist material palette relies on stone and concrete to give mass and solidity to the base and mass timber to be both the structure and spatial character of the upper level.

The pairing allows the materials to complement one another, juxtaposing lightness and weight.

“This tension between the stone base that anchors and the glulam roof that liberates is neither an aesthetic operation nor a reference to any vernacular tradition,” the studio said.

“It is a proposition about how to inhabit: what protects and what opens, what remains and what breathes, what belongs to the ground and what belongs to the air.”

Long known for concrete construction like this subtractive house in Los Angeles, PPAA has been expanding recently into mass timber design with projects like a rotating cross-laminated timber pavilion in Mexico City and Mexico’s first “all-wood” mass timber structure in Querétaro.

Architecture: PPAADesign Team: Pablo Pérez Palacios, Emilio Calvo, Miguel Vargas, Jonathan Reséndiz, Adriana Hernández Interiors: Mariana Morales

#8885. Shaw Contract Design Awards name top interiors of 2026

A Japanese office intended to evoke a tree canopy, and a revived US concert hall are among the interior design projects to win Best of Globe at this year’s Shaw Contract Design Awards.

The upgrade of an athletics clubhouse in the US, a legal workplace in the UK and a large three-story office in India also took the top prize in the annual award programme, now in its 21st year.

Held annually by flooring manufacturer Shaw Contract, the Shaw Contract Design Awards celebrate interior design projects that “spark creativity, connect communities and contribute to a better, more sustainable world”.

This year’s winning projects were selected from nearly 550 global submissions by an international jury of architects and designers, with interior design students also joining as part of Shaw’s commitment to supporting the next generation of design talent.

According to the jury, the 2026 winners were unified by “a clear design narrative, an understanding of local context, varied and inclusive user experiences, responsible material strategies and a meaningful relationship between design intent and completed space” – despite their varying scales and styles.

“Throughout the global judging session, the jury returned to a central question: whether each project’s stated intent was visible and understandable in the completed design,” explained Shaw Contract.

“The panel distinguished between attractive spaces and projects that used planning, materials, detail and experience to communicate a clear and consequential idea.”

The St Louis Symphony Orchestra Powell Hall in the US, overhauled by Christner Architects, was one of the winners.

According to Shaw Contract, the jury selected it for its sensitive balance of old and new elements, as well as the important social role it plays in the city, thanks to improved accessibility and audience facilities.

Also in the US is the winning Missouri Athletic Club project, completed by HOK. The scheme involved revamping an existing clubhouse to better suit the needs of its current members.

HOK’s design was commended for adding “a new layer to the club’s heritage rather than treating the past as a fixed visual theme”, according to the brand, introducing a contemporary layout and aesthetic.

The third winner was We Labo 25F, a small workspace in Japan that embodies the principles of biophilic design – the use of natural features such as plants to improve the wellbeing of building occupants.

Its architect, Okamura, was praised for incorporating greenery as more than just “a decorative layer” and creating an interior that mimics working beneath a tree canopy.

The office was also selected in recognition of its adaptable interiors and circular design features, including furniture made from tsunami debris.

We Labo 25F was one of three workplaces to win Best of Globe, alongside Diageo by M Moser Associates in India and DLA Piper by Sheppard Robson Architects in the UK.

Diageo spans 7,700 square metres and accommodates 300 employees across each of its three floors, accommodating its owner’s expansion from Bengaluru to Gurugram.

It was selected by the jury for its “richly layered and carefully crafted” interiors, which combine a wide range of workspaces with shared hospitality areas. M Moser Associates dedicated more than half of the building to community spaces.

Finally, DLA Piper by Sheppard Robson Architects is a large workplace for a legal company. It was designed to cater to different work styles.

According to Shaw Contract, it won the prize for providing a broad range of workspaces suited to different needs, as well as wellbeing, dining and meeting areas.

The jury particularly enjoyed how materials had been applied in a way that adds “warmth and richness into areas that might traditionally be treated as purely corporate”.

The Best of Globe winners are selected from the programme’s Best of Region winners. Winners receive global media exposure and a donation to a charity of their choice.

Shaw Contract’s ambition for the award programme is to encourage discourse within the international creative community.

#8884. Are Tangerines Good for You? 5 Health Benefits You Might Love

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:

Tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

#8883. Caá Porá Arquitectura and Jerome Haferd Studio design drum-like performance centre for Ecuador

Ecuadorian studio Caá Porá Arquitectura has teamed up with US-based Jerome Haferd Studio and engineer Juan Sebastián Pérez for the Bombódromo performance centre in Carchi, Ecuador.

The building will feature a central venue that has massive bamboo support elements based on local drums.

The campus will include dozens of buildings centred around a massive auditorium in the province of Carchi, north of Quito, sited along the Chota River in an Andean valley.

Masterplanned by Caá Porá Arquitectura, the campus was designed for local government to celebrate Afro-Ecuadorian culture.

Based on this, the central performance centre has a design based on the bomba, a drum used by local people.

“The inspiration for a lot of the design language was kind of to bridge African and Andean kind of design languages and ancestral aesthetics,” Jerome Haferd told Dezeen.

“That is embodied in the bomba drum, which is a unique instrument that is made by the people in this region, who we worked with very closely to come up with the design concept for the master plan.”

“[The bomba] was adapted and generated out of materials local to this valley in Ecuador, and so it’s really a hybrid between the Andean mountains and Africa.”

The main performance space, designed to hold more than 10,000, will have massive bundles of laminated bamboo supporting a roof system 30 metres in diameter.

These bundled columns have been designed to feature laminated bamboo and timber elements, reflecting the construction of the bomba drum and local construction methods more generally.

Acoustic fabric will hang from the wooden rafters of the semi-enclosed performance space.

A series of stone buildings will flank the main performance space, forming the back-of-house facilities.

An outdoor area will feature a tiered gathering space tucked into the low-lying trees around the river and provide the main viewing platforms for the performances.

As many as eight outbuildings will feature on the campus, including classrooms, a restaurant and artisan kiosks.

These structures will be built with metal roofs and rammed-earth walls, furthering the connection to local building techniques.

“The result is a radical, place-based reinterpretation of how a performing arts venue can respond to a unique cultural context while accommodating flexible uses,” said the team, which worked with local group Fundación Casa Oshun for the community outreach.

The project is expected to break ground in 2027.

Recently, a team including SANAA, Caá Porá Arquitectura, Estudio A0 and Jerome Haferd Studio was selected to design the National Museum of Ecuador in Quito, after the original design was cancelled following community backlash.

#8882. prefabricated timber house by NOA is designed to move with its owners

a home without a fixed address, dekruif house explores how prefabrication can offer greater flexibility in where and how people live.

Designed by NOA, DeKruif House is a prefabricated timber residence conceived for a family that does not want to commit to a single location. Originally envisioned for two waterfront sites, one in British Columbia, Canada, and another in Ilwaco, Washington, the project treats the home as something that can follow its inhabitants. Built from cross-laminated timber (CLT), the house combines a modular construction system with a distinctive arrangement of stacked volumes, circular windows, and a reflective base that connects the architecture to its surroundings.

The architects compose DeKruif House out of compact rectangular volumes stacked vertically, each slightly offset from the one below. The shifting arrangement creates a totemic silhouette while giving each floor a different relationship with the landscape. The ground level remains close to the terrain, while the upper floors offer increasingly elevated views. A circular skylight at the top completes the sequence, opening the interior directly to the sky. A scaled skin of timber shingles wraps the exterior, bringing texture and depth to the geometric composition. Circular and semicircular openings puncture the facade, breaking its rigid lines to frame selected portions of the surroundings.

The building appears to hover above the ground. Supported by slender elements, it incorporates a mirror-clad base that reflects the terrain beneath it, creating the impression that the landscape continues underneath the structure, visually reducing its presence on the site. ‘We wanted the landscape to simply carry on beneath the building. DeKruif House plays with depth, with light and shadow, and blurs the boundary between the built and the unbuilt,’ says Lukas Rungger, architect and co-founder of NOA.

Mobility is central to the conception of the project. DeKruif House uses a prefabricated CLT structure intended to adapt to different settings, subject to local conditions and building regulations. Its orientation, views, and relationship with natural light can change according to its surroundings, allowing each realization to respond to its specific location.

Placed on a larger boat, the structure can become a movable houseboat, offering another possibility for families who prefer not to establish a permanent home in one place. Three configurations, measuring 45, 60, and 75 square meters of net internal area, provide different spatial arrangements, with additional bedrooms and bathrooms possible without changing the underlying architectural concept.

A complementary element is DeKruif Island, a small circular outdoor space conceived as a private garden. It accommodates a hot tub, a shaded tree, seating areas, and a central fireplace, creating an outdoor room that extends the domestic experience into the surrounding landscape. ‘DeKruif Island is a little circular outdoor room with a hot tub, a tree for shade, places to sit and a fireplace at its centre. It is a private garden that brings you even closer to nature,’ Rungger explains.

Τhe vertical arrangement of the house creates intimate spaces connected by a spiral staircase that runs through the structure. Inside, the exposed CLT gives the rooms a consistent look, with the natural grain of the timber left visible and finishes kept simple.

The living and kitchen area forms the main gathering space, organized around a suspended fireplace. Large openings connect it to the terrace, extending everyday activities towards the outdoors. Bedrooms occupy the upper levels, where the circular windows establish more private and individual relationships with the surroundings. In the bathroom, a freestanding bathtub faces one of these openings, turning the landscape into part of the bathing experience.

‘Inside, we balance the sculptural exterior with calm. The house oscillates between openness and enclosure, dark and bright, cold and warm, wet and dry, inside and out. Rather than opening up the whole facade, every window frames one specific view: we embrace the panorama by framing it,’ Rungger notes.

#8881. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

#8880. Sumayya Vally to design Dubai art foundation around the "memory of a house"

South African architect Sumayya Vally is designing a permanent home for the Elie Khouri Art Foundation (EKAF), which will be located within a renovated villa in Dubai.

Set to be built in the Jumeirah 1 development in Dubai, the foundation’s home will be located in a former villa, which will be dramatically overhauled by Vally – principal of architecture studio Counterspace.

“I think of buildings as having many lives,” said Vally. “At EKAF, we begin with a house that has already held a world within it. Its doors, cornices, balustrades, and particular ways of receiving people and separating rooms contain the traces of another life,” she continued.

“I am interested in what happens when we take these intimate geometries and give them a new public scale: when the architecture of a room becomes the architecture of a city-facing facade, and the memory of a house becomes the beginnings of an institution.”

Although few details of the design have been revealed, a render shows what appears to be a three-storey building with a light pink textured facade.

Lines across the facade appear to suggest fragments of the previous building, with recognisable shapes including doorways visible. Geometric holes punched in the facade will reveal activities taking place inside.

EKAF was established by Lebanese-French businessman Elie Khouri and its permanent home is planned to open in 2028. The foundation will contain gallery space to show its permanent collection and will also include space for temporary exhibits.

“I hope that artists, designers, researchers and makers from the region will bring other imaginations into the work, and that the institution will continue to acquire forms and meanings we cannot yet anticipate,” added Vally.

Designer of the Serpentine Pavilion in 2021, Vally was named emerging architect of the year at Dezeen Awards in 2023 and one of Time magazine’s 100 leaders of the future in 2021.

#8879. Five little-known stage designs from the archives of Zaha Hadid

Photography by Luke Hayes unless stated otherwise

The unsung set designs of Zaha Hadid take centre stage in the latest exhibition curated by her foundation in London. In this roundup, we spotlight five standout objects that were uncovered from her archives for the show.

Named Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance, the exhibition is the Zaha Hadid Foundation‘s first collection-based show dedicated to the architect’s portfolio of stage and set designs.

It coincides with the reopening of the foundation’s home in Hadid’s former office – a former Victorian schoolhouse at 10 Bowling Green Lane in Clerkenwell, following a refurbishment by Studio KA coinciding with the 10th anniversary of Hadid’s passing.

The exhibition was curated by the foundation’s senior researcher Catherine Howe and design historian Libby Sellers as guest curator, and contains five projects illustrated through a mix of archival models, drawings, video footage and even costume.

Together, these offer insight into the evolution of Hadid’s signature complex geometries and digital design techniques, through the lens of sets for dance, opera and pop music.

According to curator Howe, the exhibition exemplifies how Hadid “didn’t want to be fixed” in her work, and how “she wanted to work across so many media”.

Howe added that the exhibition came about serendipitously, after the foundation had kept discovering records of these unsung projects while unpacking boxes.

“We open a lot of boxes,” she told Dezeen during a tour of the exhibition. “Sometimes it’s fortuitous, or it’s that there’s a big box and we need to move it, and we kept noticing all these amazing projects that hadn’t really been talked about.”

“Of course, everyone talks about her incredible buildings, but I think the interdisciplinarity of some of these projects was just being forgotten about, and we said ‘we need to do something on performance’.”

The foundation’s chairman, Rana Hadid, who is also the niece of Hadid, told Dezeen the reopening of the foundation was a “very emotional” moment for her, but suggested the exhibition only marks the beginning of discovering treasures in the foundation’s archive, which is estimated to contain 300,000 items.

“[Hadid’s] archive is so extraordinary, it’s limitless paintings, drawings, sketchbooks, digital material, personal material, it goes way beyond architecture,” Rana Hadid explained.

“It’s really about studying the process of her thinking, and using all that to help younger generations learn more about the process, the experimentation, the way you can start an idea and move forward with it, use technologies to be able to build it.”

The Zaha Hadid Foundation is an independent charity founded by Hadid in 2013. The Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance exhibition is on until 27 March 2027.

The foundation’s reopening programme also includes a video artwork by artist LionHeart and a timeline visualisation of Hadid’s life by data journalist Mona Chalabi.

Read on for five stand-out exhibits from the Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance exhibition.

Hadid created this model for her design for the staging of Mozart’s Così fan tutte opera, presented at Frank Gehry’s Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles in 2014.

Her dynamic stage design featured a spiralling white platform, engineered with sections that could rise and fall to help echo the shifting relationships of performers in the opera.

It had a curvature that mirrors many of her buildings, including the iconic Heydar Aliyev Centre in Baku, completed two years prior.

Another model featured in the exhibition is one Hadid created when designing the set for the Pet Shop Boys’ Nightlife World Tour, which took place between 1999 and 2000.

The design comprised an interconnected, reconfigurable system of ramps that could be tailored to suit different venues while maintaining the overall aesthetic. It also incorporated projection surfaces, transforming the stage into a multimedia environment.

According to the foundation, it was Hadid’s “first commission for a major pop concert”.

This collection of digital drawings depicts the stage design that Hadid created for the Metapolis Ballet in 1999, and embodies the abstract design language for which the architect was best known.

These ultimately became a trio of lightweight bridge structures that were moved, reconfigured and even worn by dancers across the stage. It is exhibited alongside a costume, which Hadid also designed for the ballet.

This trio of models were developed by Hadid for her pavilion at an event in Groningen called What a Wonderful World! Music Videos in Architecture in 1990.

It responded to a brief that asked for explorations into how the cultural phenomenon of music videos could be translated from screen to public space.

Hadid’s final design featured an uncharacteristically bright colour palette and a grid-like structure with shifting floors and angular walkways, and proposed “how architecture could shape the experience of viewing itself”, the foundation said.

The final pavilion was exhibited alongside contributions by her fellow ‘deconstructivist’ architects, including Rem Koolhaas, Bernard Tschumi, Peter Eisenman, and Coop Himmelb(l)au.

This abstract sketch of an unnamed architectural project, originally developed by Hadid for Hamburg, later formed the basis of a dance performance called d1 by British choreographer Rosemary Butcher.

The project, which was Hadid’s first dedicated to performance, saw the sketch transformed into a monochromatic network of lines on a floor, across which dancers moved as though “navigating a cityscape”.

Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance takes place from 3 November 2026 to Saturday 27 March 2027. For more events in architecture and design, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

#8878. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.
